author: Dannish Odongo
title: The Other Side of Scotland: Humaneness at Home, Barbarity Abroad
content:
I was walking past the University of Stirling’s Airthrey Loch when I saw a young Scottish man fishing at its edge. As a son of the lake, who grew up next to Nam Lolwe, renamed Lake Victoria by the colonizer, I was automatically drawn to it. So when I saw the rod, the line, the stillness and anticipation of someone waiting for the water to dictate their next steps, I had to stop and join the man in this quiet business which our people consider sacred.


He was patient, almost signalling that he had done this many times. The rod was held loosely. His eyes were on the water, waiting, not pushing. Then the line went taut. It happened quickly. The rod bent. His feet shifted. Veins popped out of his neck and hands as his arms pulled against something that was pulling back. The fish did not come easily. For several minutes they argued about it. Then, by some combination of his muscles and his equipment, the fish came ashore. It was large and golden, a brown trout, solid and carnivorous, built for the cold Scottish water. It reminded me immediately of the

mumi

 we used to catch as boys when the flooded fields of Kano brought them close, sometimes to our living rooms. Using torches, we would lure them close enough to grab them from the shallow water.


The young man set the fish on the bank and reached for a measuring tape. While it was twisting, gulping for air, he measured it carefully, noted the length, and made a record of it. No sooner had he laid it on the bank than a uniformed man, who looked like a security person, arrived. Cordial, unhurried, he asked to see the permit. A permit, to fish in a university loch, with a single line, for a single fish, on a weekday. He produced it with ease. He had collected it from the university before coming to the loch, because in this country a permit is simply part of going fishing, and you carry it the way you carry a fishing bag.


Then he put the fish back in the water.


That is the expectation here, at least in this loch. You catch it. Measure it. Record it. Return it.


A few minutes after he had left, I was still standing there, processing what I had just witnessed, especially as a man who was fresh in this country and had not been fully oriented in their ways, including this legislated kindness to animals.


In Kano, we fished in small rivers and tributaries because the fish was dinner. Here, the fish is the point. The eating is incidental, or absent entirely. And it made me think about this particular kind of prosperity that produces this, a society so far past the question of whether there will be food tonight that it has arrived at an entirely different relationship with the natural world.


But the same country that legislates this loch also has one of the largest fishing fleets in the world. British trawlers move through the North Atlantic and beyond, dragging nets across ocean floors, pulling up more in a single trip than a thousand Kano fishermen would catch in a lifetime. I wondered about that. About whether the careful angler and the industrial trawler can really be part of the same moral story, or whether one exists, in some quiet way, to make the other easier to live with. It also made me think about how the media routinely covers the floods of Kano and their devastating impact. But no one has asked why the fish stopped coming. Why only a foul stench now accompanies the seasonal floods.


It was late October, the tail end of autumn. The sky was grey and heavy over the Ochil Hills. The trees were losing their leaves. The darkness was arriving earlier each day, not yet the full winter dark, but you could feel it gathering. The University of Stirling sits on three hundred and sixty acres of parkland at the foot of those hills, built on the grounds of Airthrey Castle, an eighteenth-century estate whose giant redwoods, oak, beech and birch still line the paths between the buildings. Squirrels run between them without breaking stride. Swans move across the loch as if they own it, because in every way that matters, they do.


I had been noticing other things too, but I didn’t yet have the words to describe them.


Disturbing sheep is illegal


On the paths near a large farm estate near Bridge of Allan, there are signs warning that disturbing sheep is an offence and dogs found doing that will be shot. Standing next to one of those signs, I asked myself: who decides which animals get the sign? Who decides which people get removed to make room for the animals that now …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Marikana’s wounds still bleed 14 years after police massacre
content:
Fourteen years after police opened fire on striking mineworkers at Marikana, the massacre is remembered not only for the 34 men who were killed, but for their absence in the lives of their families.


For some, the memory is of a father who never came home. For others, it is the loss of a breadwinner, a brother or a son. And for those who were children when the killings happened, it is the experience of growing up with memories that have become increasingly distant, while the questions about justice remain.


At a commemoration marking 14 years since the massacre, the families, activists and academics reflected on what Marikana means more than a decade later – and on its place in South Africa’s longer history of protest, police violence and struggles for dignity.


For the Socio-Economic Rights Institute of South Africa (Seri), which has represented the families since 2012, the central question remains accountability. Seri secured payments for 35 of the 37 families whose loved ones were killed by police. Two families have received no compensation.


Seri’s executive director, Nomzamo Zondo said the compensation process itself reflected a deeper problem in how the state understood the loss suffered by the families. “Part of that is a narrative that what the state is interested in compensating is the income that the miners would have earned. They do not want to account for the husbands, brothers, sons and fathers that they took away from the families,” she said.


For Zondo, compensation alone cannot address the significance of Marikana. The state also needs to acknowledge that the massacre should never have happened, she argued: “That’s what a public holiday on the 16

th

 of August would mean. It would say: we are saying never, never again.”


She said this was particularly important given the continued use of force by police in managing protests. “We’ve seen that police continue to manage protests through the use of violence. They have continuously refused to accept that their role is to facilitate protests as a constitutional right.”


Zondo also pointed to the failure to implement recommendations made by the panel of experts on public order policing and the management of protests. The panel completed its work in 2018, but its recommendations remain largely unimplemented.


Squalid living conditions in the informal settlement, Nkaneng, in the shadow of Marikana platinum mine, a source of immense wealth for the owners in 2012, Lonmin. Archive photo by The Benchmarks Foundation


Another major concern, she said, was the failure of the National Prosecuting Authority to bring those responsible for the 16 August killings to court. “Every year, of course, when the anniversary comes, there is an explanation that work is being done,” Zondo said. “But now we are like one year short from 15 years since the massacre. We are just 12 years since the Commission finalised its report and recommended that the NPA must investigate and charge whoever is responsible.”


The question, she said, was whether there was “really an intention to hold anyone accountable for the deaths of the 16

th

 of August”.


For the families, however, the consequences of Marikana are not measured only by the progress of criminal investigations or compensation claims. They are lived in the absence of loved ones.


‘I still have that memory’


NowilI Nungu was 15 when her father, Jackson Lehopa, was killed at Marikana. Today, at 29, she remembers him through the ordinary moments of their life together: travelling to school on a bicycle, buying him a Coke and watching him repair the bicycle whenever it broke.


“I have so many memories with my dad,” Nungu said. She was the only girl among six children and had been living with her father in Rustenburg while her mother moved back to the Eastern Cape.


By the time of the massacre, Nungu had moved to the Eastern Cape with her mother. The family did not have electricity and relied on the radio for news. Her father normally called every day after returning from the koppie to tell them he was safe. But that day, he did not call.


Crosses erected at the koppie as a symbol of lives lost on 16 August 2012. Archive photo by Muzi Mzoyi


Sebolai Liau lost his father, the late Janefeke Raphael Liau, at Marikana. For him, the question of justice remains unresolved. “I think regarding the Marikana massacre, there is no justice. I don’t think it will ever be served, but for now it has not been, and there are no signs …

author: Abahlali_3
title: This August we honour the women of South Africa
content:
11 August 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

This August we honour the women of South Africa

This August, in women’s month, we speak of the comrades who are mothers, daughters, sisters and grandmothers, comrades who wake up every morning in the shack settlements and carry the weight of a country that has forgotten them.

We honour the women who keep their families going under conditions of brutal impoverishment and the women who resist oppression. We honour the women in our movement.

But this is not a month of celebration.

No woman is fully free in South Africa. All women are at risk of violence. Impoverished women remain profoundly oppressed.

There is no celebration when women continue to live under very dangerous conditions.

There is no celebration when a woman must walk to a communal tap after dark and risk rape or attack.

There is no celebration when there is no electricity, no running water, no toilets, and no safety for children.

There is no celebration when a woman does not know if her home will be standing tomorrow because of evictions, fires, or political violence.

For millions of impoverished women in shacks, tin houses and backyards, every day is a fight for survival.

To celebrate while all this is true is to lie.

This August we honour all the women of our movement who refused to accept poverty as fate.

We honour Nqobile Nzuza who was murdered by a police officer on a road blockade in Cato Crest on 30 September 2013. She was seventeen years old and doing her matric. She joined the road blockade in protest against the brutal attacks on the Marikana Land Occupation in Cato Manor by the eThekwini Municipality. She was committed to the struggle for land.

We honour Comrade Thuli Ndlovu, a leader of Abahlali baseMjondolo in KwaNdengezi. She fought for land, for housing, and for the dignity of her community. She was assassinated on 27 September 2014 for confronting oppression.

We honour Comrade Nokuthula Mabaso, a leader of eKhenana Commune and of the Abahlali Women’s League. She was a mother, an organiser, and a builder of a community that fed itself and governed itself. She was assassinated on 5 May 2022 while her community was under attack. She knew that poor people must seize the right to land and to live with dignity.

Our brave comrades refused oppression and insisted on land and dignity. Thuli and Nokuthula were leaders.

We also honour other women who have given their lives in the struggle for justice.

Fikile Ntshangase was a leading member of the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (MCEJO) which opposed the destruction of people’s land and homes by coal mining. She was assassinated on 22 October 2020.

Babita Deokaran was an honest civil servant and a whistleblower in the Gauteng Department of Health. She exposed corruption and the theft of public money meant for the public hospitals and clinics that serve the poor. She was assassinated in 2021 for refusing to look away as powerful and dangerous men looted the healthcare system.

We have no interest in politicians who come with speeches and flowers and say nothing about the oppression we live today and nothing about our leaders who have given their lives in the struggle against this oppression.

1.⁠ ⁠Secure access to land and decent housing so no woman sleeps in fear of eviction or fire. 2.⁠ Access to basic services such as water, electricity, sanitation, and safe public lighting in every settlement. 3.⁠ ⁠An end to political killings and intimidation of women organisers. 4.⁠ ⁠An end to gender-based violence in homes, streets, schools and communities. 5.⁠ ⁠Decent work, healthcare and education so women are not forced to choose between feeding their children and their own health. 6. Reproductive healthcare and contraception available without humiliation or delay. 7. A livable guaranteed income in recognition of the unpaid care work that holds families and communities together. 8. Decisive action to reduce food prices on essential items. 9. An end to attempts to turn poor women against migrant and refugee women, since the enemy is landlessness, unemployment and state neglect, not our neighbours. 10.⁠ ⁠Accountability for the killings of Nqobile, Thuli, Nokuthula, Fikile, Babita and all the other murdered and assassinated women activists whose cases were closed and forgotten.

Poor women are not asking to be celebrated. We are demanding to be safe, to be housed, to be heard, to be alive.

Until that happens, August …

author: William Shoki
title: On Safari
content:
Ever since the

World Cup

 concluded with Spain’s emphatic triumph over universally loathed Argentina (at least it felt this way), it has no longer felt like everyone is looking in the same direction at the same time. For a month and a bit, football’s biggest stage gave us one of the last remaining experiences of shared, global time. Not global justice, not global equality — the tournament is in many ways a monument to their absence — but a crude, synchronized schedule. Games at set hours, short-lived solidarities, the impression, however false, that the world is briefly doing something together, undergoing a collective experience.

Once that all ends, you’re plunged back into a social temporality and news cycle that moves at lightning speed and adjusting back is disorienting. It didn’t help that I had to deal with a debilitating case of

cyclosporiasis

 (in an ill-fated decision, I tried some Taco Bell for the first time the day before my return flight back to South Africa, and getting a food-borne illness felt like an appropriate parting gift from a United States in decline). In the weeks since the World Cup, I found myself in a kind of fog I at first attributed to being exhausted from a busy year coupled with bouts of illness, but which, as I return to relatively decent health, I recognize as a familiar feeling, one that has typified contemporary experience for as long as I can remember.

There’s a book by the Polish sociologist Zygmunt Bauman which I think is underrated, and does better at capturing the texture of our epoch than many other attempts (do we live in late capitalism, surveillance capitalism, the burnout society, post-modernity, etc etc.). It’s called

Liquid Modernity

, and Bauman’s straightforward argument is that the defining feature of contemporary society is no longer the construction of stable institutions, identities, and social relationships, but their constant dissolution. Where the “solid” phase of modernity sought to build enduring structures — stable careers, lifelong marriages, nation-states, political parties, class identities, and fixed moral frameworks — our present condition is “liquid”: forms no longer retain their shape for long enough to organize human life. The contradictory result of this is that even though in many important respects, individuals have unprecedented freedom (at least compared to any other point in human history), it’s coupled with chronic insecurity and the burden of constantly having to remake ourselves.

One of his most evocative concepts is the notion of pointillist time, which is “more prominent for its inconsistency and lack of cohesion than for its elements of continuity and consistency.” Time under liquid modernity is fragmented and disconnected, and rather than unfolding as a series of events with some relationship to each other, it is rather a series of “eternal instants.” It’s not hard work to see how this characterizes so much of algorithm-dominated society in general, and our media consumption in particular. If it wasn’t hard enough figuring out what producing any meaningful “content” takes in the attention economy, it was dismaying for me to recently learn that even new media like podcasts and video essays are themselves now being repurposed in a

“clipping economy”

 where increasingly, circulation of short clips from longer pieces is becoming the main event rather than previews.

At

Africa Is a Country

, we are very proud of our World Cup Road Trip series. Three episodes are live —

Episode 1

 on the Cabo Verdean diaspora in New England,

Episode 2

 on the affinity between Algeria and Lawrence, Kansas, and

Episode 3

 on Toronto’s Ghanaian community — with further episodes from the road currently in post-production. Although the website and our weekly newsletters remain our bread and butter, like most outlets, we are experimenting with different ways of reaching audiences, and short-form video has been one of them. The newsletter in particular functions as our most reliable direct channel to readers as social platform referrals grow less dependable. The World Cup, however, gave us a powerful on-ramp: sport brought in readers who might not otherwise arrive at a piece on visa regimes or xenophobia, and the coverage was built to convert that interest into political understanding.

What has been challenging is that discovery is now heavily platform-dependent, and the same work travels very differently depending on where it lands: our road trip …

author: Mostafa Hosny
title: Why prescribe drugs by brand name? Pharmacists call for change after child endangered by drug dispensing error
content:
Last week, seven-year-old Mecca came down with a cold and a sore throat. She visited her doctor for examination, and was prescribed a nutritional supplement to help with the symptoms. Her family sent a photo of the prescription to a pharmacy in Zahraa al-Maadi for home delivery, and the drug was delivered around 11:30 pm.


After ingesting a 6-ml dose of the drug, however, Mecca “suffered something akin to paralysis,” her mother, Samia, tells Mada Masr.


“My daughter was suffering from a simple cold,” says Samia. “But the pharmacist confused the last two letters [of the drug’s name] and dispensed an epilepsy medication instead.”


Samia rushed her daughter to the Poison Control Center, which refused to admit Mecca, as did several hospitals afterward, with all of them telling the mother that, since it had been 24 hours since the medication was administered, she needed to go to the intensive care unit at Demerdash Hospital, where the specialized care unit is located. 


Mecca remained sick for a day and a half, “no longer able to move her hands, legs or eyes,” Samia says. She remained in this condition for four days before eventually recovering.


Soon after the life-threatening incident, the family filed a lawsuit against the pharmacy and submitted complaints to the Egyptian Drug Authority — the body responsible for pharmacy inspections — as well as to the Pharmacists Syndicate and the public prosecutor. 


But professionals working in the pharmacy sector and syndicate officials who spoke to Mada Masr say Mecca’s case is not the first time a patient has faced dangerous consequences as a result of mistakes in interpreting prescriptions. 


For them, complaints and investigations into each individual incident — while important for establishing liability and holding the responsible party accountable — will fail to address the root cause of the problem or prevent its recurrence, leaving patients exposed to the same danger.


They believe the true solution lies in changing prescribing practices: mandating that physicians prescribe medications by their generic, non-proprietary names to reduce the likelihood that pharmacists will confuse the commercial names of popular drugs, a demand that pharmacists have put to the Health Ministry in recent days and which has already been

recommended

 in a 2024 prime ministerial directive.


However, doctors have expressed unwillingness to adhere to the recommendation — a stance that several sources who spoke to Mada Masr attribute to the

strong financial and professional incentives

 offered by pharmaceutical companies to doctors, part of marketing arrangements that generate billions in revenue. 


***


Mistakes in drug dispensation of the kind that endangered Samia’s daughter are easily made when doctors prescribe drugs by their commercial name, according to two pharmacists who spoke to Mada Masr.


A Pharmacists Syndicate official, speaking on condition of anonymity, tells Mada Masr that Mecca would not have been endangered had the generic name been used. The confusion originated due to a confusion between the name of the prescribed drug and a different drug with a similar name, he says.


“The active ingredient in the first medication, Acetylcysteine, is completely different from the one in the second medication, Risperidone, which is used to treat certain psychiatric and neurological disorders,” he explains. 


A pharmacy manager notes that by contrast the trade name for the prescribed drug, Respidep, is very similar to Risperdal, the brand name of the antipsychotic that was dispensed.


“Similar incidents have occurred many times,” says the pharmacy manager. “One case that stands out in my memory involved a pharmacist who mistakenly dispensed a neurological medication: the difference between the name written on the prescription and the drug actually dispensed was just two letters.”


A bare minimum threshold to prevent the recurrence of similar incidents would be to mandate that doctors use generic names, says the manager, who stresses that “there is no active ingredient whose name resembles another active ingredient in the way brand names do.” 


Brand names, by contrast, are frequently very similar, he says, noting that companies will often exploit the name recognition of existing medication, launching drugs under similar brand names that differ by a couple of letters.


There are myriad examples of similar trade names, such as antispasmodic drugs Spasomofin and Spasmomen, or …

author: Ahmed Ismat
title: Sudan: The Unfortunate Alliance
content:
On Foreign Interest, the Ideal Militia, and What a Coloniser Prays He Leaves Behind


My grandmother never said displacement. She said: we left the house and the water took it. But the water did not take it. The state took it. A state that had been making that decision for decades, in different languages, with different flags.


My grandfather Ahmed was an English teacher in Halfa Dagheim, a Nubian town on the Nile near the Egyptian border. In the 1960s, a decision was made far away—in Cairo, with Soviet engineers drawing designs, and American dollars quietly approving—to build the Aswan High Dam. The dam needed a reservoir; the reservoir needed our valley. My grandfather and his neighbors were given promises and a dusty strip of land in Wadi Halfa. The first thing the families built together under a tree was a school, with my grandfather at its centre.


Ahmed Mohammed Khalil Bairum school in Wadi Halfa, established by the author’s grandfather after the original community in Halfa was displaced by the Aswan High Dam.


My grandfather died before I was old enough to ask him how you build a school when you have just lost a town. My mother inherited that grief, carrying it while studying veterinary medicine at the University of Khartoum. She graduated with me in her arms. What happened to my grandfather was not an accident. A state decided that a reservoir mattered more than a family. What kind of state makes that decision repeatedly?


* * *


There is a particular fantasy that all empires share. When direct control becomes too expensive, leave behind a local manager who will do the work without the embarrassment—the militia as outsourced violence with deniability built in.


At first, the Rapid Support Forces looks like a local story. But when Hemedti’s soldiers drove into Khartoum on 15 April 2023, they arrived from a long chain of decisions made in Washington, London, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi, Moscow, and Brussels.


The British arrived in 1898 to grow cotton for Lancashire. They built the Gezira scheme around a state designed for extraction resting on four pillars: generals to suppress workers, militia leaders to discipline tenant farmers, capital owners, and politicians to explain the arrangement to London. They also left a legal architecture: the Vagrancy Act criminalised movement without permission, creating a category of people who were poor in the wrong place without a permit. When the British left, a clique of Sudanese men inherited the machine. Six days after independence, tenant farmers in Jouda went on strike; the army surrounded the village and killed over three hundred people. The rifle was the same.


* * *


After independence, that inherited machine discovered it was valuable to other people. Following the 1979 Iranian Revolution, Riyadh and Washington flooded the region with funds to build a Sunni counterweight. In Sudan, the vehicle was the Muslim Brotherhood, and the financial anchor was the Faisal Islamic Bank—operating tax-free under a special charter outside normal banking regulations. The bank bankrolled the regime, funded partly by mortgaging University of Khartoum land. Students paid tuition to a fund that paid loans to a bank that financed the teargas fired at us. That is what foreign interest looks like at the human level.


The IMF is a more patient kind of foreign interest, arriving with spreadsheets. From 1978 onward, through dictatorships and brief democracies, every government received the same prescription: cut subsidies, devalue, privatise. Each government repeated: there is no alternative. When fuel subsidies were removed in 2013, and bread in 2018, prices doubled overnight; tires burned; revolutions started. In 2021, Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok stood in Khartoum and repeated the phrase, implementing a devastating 55-to-375 exchange-rate shock required to access fifty billion dollars in debt relief.


When the state retreats from subsidy, it leaves a vacuum. In the Soba industrial zone, a biscuit factory paid 1,500 Sudanese Pounds (SDG; equivalent to 3 pounds sterling) for a twelve-hour shift, while rent in Haj Yousif was 30,000 pounds. When the RSF offered 15,000 SDG (£30) a day plus a uniform and a phone, young men joined. That is not ideology; that is arithmetic. A person trying to survive is not a symbol—he is just someone the structure needs to keep moving in a circle.


* * *


Follow that arithmetic west. Colonial planners designed Darfur not for production, but as a buffer to …

author: Noziphiwo Sigwela
title: Public land for the public good: Tafelberg ruling puts Cape Town on notice
content:
On the 2

nd

 of July 2026, the Constitutional Court handed down an unanimous judgement that will reshape how we understand the right to housing in South Africa.


The Tafelberg judgment (

Adonisi v Minister for Transport and Public Works, Western Cape; Minister of Human Settlements v Minister for Transport and Public Works, Western Cape

 [2026] ZACC 29 (2 July 2026)

) declared the 2015 sale of the Tafelberg property at 353 Main Road, Sea Point, Cape Town, unlawful.


This ruling highlighted the failure by the Western Cape government and City of Cape Town to fulfil their constitutional duties to redress spatial injustice by providing affordable housing in well-located areas. This battle was championed by urban land movement,

Reclaim the City

, with support from NGO,

Ndifuna Ukwazi

. In a celebrated outcome, both levels of government were ordered to submit detailed reports to the high court within three months (2 October 2026).


But as we celebrate this victory, we must confront the sobering truth. This was only one of the City’s many failures. The same week the Constitutional Court affirmed the importance of spatial justice, the Public Protector released a devastating report on the City’s failure to provide basic municipal services to Langa Flats in Langa and in the township of Khayelitsha. The contrast could not be clearer. While the city and provincial governments fought for a decade to sell off prime public land in Sea Point, residents in Langa and Khayelitsha have been living without functioning sewers, fire safety equipment, clean water, and without the dignity that the constitution promises them.


Two cities, one constitution


The Public Protector’s report,

Systemic Investigation into Alleged Failure by the City of Cape Town to Provide Basic Municipal Services in Langa Flats and Khayelitsha Township

, reads like an indictment of a city that has forgotten half its residents.


In Langa Flats, sewer infrastructure has been in a state of disrepair for 14 years. Firehose reels and extinguishers that were promised to be repaired in March 2022 are still broken.


Residents have been forced to contribute R100 per household to hire cleaners for communal areas, a responsibility that rightfully belongs to the municipality. Housing units have cracked walls that, despite repeated commitments, are years later still to be assessed.


According to the report by the Public Protector, Town Two Clinic does not have smoke detectors or CCTV cameras. Earlier this year, the security company at the clinic fell victim to extortion rackets that are ravaging the community.


In Khayelitsha, the picture is no better. At SST-Marikana, residents who were relocated by the City to make way for sewer repairs were moved to a site without access to electricity or adequate water.


In multiple inspections of the area, the Public Protector found none of the 143 water taps that the City claimed to have provided. Relocated families relied on a self-connected communal tap – a pipe pressed down with a cement block, providing only a trickle of water.


An elderly wheelchair-bound resident was left alone without accessible water or electricity, in conditions “neither safe nor conducive to his health and wellbeing”.


At the

Matthew Goniwe

 and

Town Two

 clinics, there were no smoke detectors, and no functional CCTV cameras, with paper records stored in rooms without fire detection. Staff at

Matthew Goniwe

 reported that the clinic could go without electricity for two to three weeks at a time. This is not a failure of resources alone, but a failure of

priorities

.


The spatial logic of neglect


What connects Tafelberg to Langa and Khayelitsha is not just geography but a spatial logic that has persisted since Apartheid. Well-located land in Sea Point is fiercely protected for the wealthy, while poor and working-class communities are pushed to the urban periphery and are neglected there – out of sight, out of mind!


The Constitutional Court’s Tafelberg judgment recognised this explicitly. Justice Mhlantla, in her judgment, said that the location of housing must be treated as a “relevant factor” in decisions about public land, particularly where such decisions affect efforts to redress apartheid spatial injustice.


But spatial justice is not only about where housing is built, it is also about how communities are

served

 once they are there. The Public Protector’s report reveals a pattern of systematic neglect that mirrors the …

author: Nabil Ferdaoussi
title: A border spectacle
content:
What happened last Thursday in Ceuta was a

border spectacle

 of surprising scale and scope. Tens of thousands of mainly young fellow Moroccans stormed the gates while others braved the water to enter the enclave. All the elements of the spectacle were there: from images of boisterous youngsters jockeying for entry, to a diplomatic slanging match, to border patrols scrambling to push migrants back to Morocco.

It sounds like a geopolitical déjà vu — almost the same border antics: scene, actors, protagonists, and victims staged in May 2021. In fact, what happened in Ceuta is the third episode of the border spectacle: the first staged in May 2021, the second in September 2024, and here we are watching the third — and perhaps not the last — episode, marking a shift in Morocco’s migration diplomacy to a more coercive approach.

There is no conspiracy theory behind the Ceuta border spectacle; there is only a geopolitical buildup to understand Morocco’s coercive migration diplomacy. The latter has shifted migration governance from policies, practices, and discourses to the direct use of its youth and other racialized African migrants in diplomatic sparring.

Here is the buildup: On December 10, 2020, the Trump administration recognized Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara. This historic moment led Morocco to garner further diplomatic recognition, especially from its traditional allies — not least Spain as a former colonizer. In January 2021, a diplomatic logjam between Morocco and Germany started to simmer following the latter’s criticism of Donald Trump’s proclamation to recognize Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. This diplomatic friction with Germany prompted Morocco to push the European Union.

Meanwhile, the possibility of meeting Morocco’s expectations, whether by the EU or its member states, proved far-fetched. The diplomatic spat between Morocco and Spain reached its nadir when the latter hosted Brahim Ghali, the leader of the Polisario Front, in April 2021 to seek medical treatment. In a tit-for-tat response, Morocco unleashed over 8,000 migrants, including around 3,000 minors. Santiago Abascal, the leader of the anti-migrant far-right Vox party in Spain, denounced the arrivals, stating Morocco was “launching minors like battering rams” against the Spanish borders.

Now, the same scenario is unfolding after Pedro Sánchez visited Algeria to parley with President Abdelmajid Tebboune over natural gas and Western Sahara.

In Europe, the border spectacle sparked a moral panic that feared the invasion of the southern flanks of Europe, raking up right-wing opprobrium over Sánchez’s progressive yet lax migration policies. Far from being an invasion, the border spectacle staged produced anti-migration fodder for far-right politicians.

The border spectacle has resurfaced the centuries-old colonization of Ceuta and Melilla.

The international public that redeems Sánchez as the proponent of the Palestinian cause and progressive migration reforms is bewildered by Ceuta’s tiny geography at the outer fringe of the African continent, wondering how Spain, and for that matter Europe, will be invaded while in Africa. Some historical context is urgent here to disentangle these “only land borders between Africa and EUrope.”

Depending on one’s geopolitical stance, Ceuta and Melilla are at once enclaves and exclaves. From the colonial standpoint of Spain and the European Union, they are seen as exclaves, embodying the external sovereign extension of Spain and, more recently, Europe. In most academic literature, however, the two cities are enclaves standing as the last remnants of European colonization on the African continent. For Moroccans, the two cities are occupied territories, whose recovery remains an unfinished national project of decolonization.

The dispute over Ceuta and Melilla has shaped a long history of sporadic tensions in the relationship between Morocco and Spain. Its historical roots extend back to the Reconquista (c. 718–1492), culminating in the fall of Al-Andalus, and ended with the expulsion of the Moors, between 718 and 1492, from the Iberian Peninsula to North Africa.

Spain extended its sovereignty beyond the Peninsula to vie for external territorial sovereignty in North Africa, seizing Melilla in 1497 and Ceuta — initially conquered by Portugal in 1415 and then ceded to Spain — in 1668. The two towns served as external bulwarks for the clash between the

Ummah

 of Islam and Christendom. Well …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Premier optimistic ahead of Canada-U.S trade deal deadline
content:
Nunavut Premier John Main says he feels “encouraged” by the progress in trade negotiations as yet another tariff deadline looms Friday at midnight.


Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and Canada’s lead negotiator Janice Charette are in Washington, D.C., to negotiate a new Canada-U.S.-Mexico, or CUSMA, trade agreement with U.S. officials such as trade representative Jamieson Greer.


Canada is trying to avert a new round of tariffs that U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened on nearly $30 billion of Canadian goods if a new deal isn’t reached. At issue is the export of American milk and sale of American liquor north of the border, among other items.


“Although there are still several outstanding issues under active consideration, I’m confident that these efforts will lead to a mutually beneficial agreement,” Main said Thursday in a statement to Nunatsiaq News.


He said a new deal stands to strengthen supply chains that “matter deeply in northern and remote communities,” and that he feels optimistic it can be achieved.


But any deal would need to take into account “unique pressures” Nunavut is facing, like affordability, Main said, pointing to transportation costs, greater supply chain vulnerability, and the high cost of living.


“No single agreement solves everything,” he said.

“Our government is focused on making sure the North is part of the economic benefits that come from a strong and stable trade relationship.”


Prime Minister Mark Carney updated premiers Wednesday on the talks and urged them to restock American alcohol in their liquor stores.


Main said he’s ready to comply so that American products can be available for purchase again in Nunavut. 


“Whether Canadians want to buy American alcohol is up to them,” the premier added.


Former Nunavut premier

P.J. Akeeagok is also advocating for the territory as part of Carney’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations.


Akeeagok is the only Inuk voice on the committee and previously stated his goal is to put the Arctic at the “centre of Canada’s strategic investment agenda and at the forefront of nation‑building.” 


“I have consistently emphasized the central importance of the Arctic to Canada’s sovereignty, security, defence posture, and critical minerals strategy,” Akeeagok shared in a short written statement to Nunatsiaq News.


“We hold significant opportunities for the country, and Inuit regions have a great deal to offer in shaping Canada’s long‑term economic and strategic position.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Hind Rajab’s Family Says Israel’s Investigation Into Hind’s Death Just a PR Ploy
content:
“Even now, all I hear is her crying, ‘I’m scared,’ and her plea: ‘Come here, Mama, take me,’” Hind’s mother said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Hind Rajab’s mother has dismissed the Israeli military’s announcement this week that it is opening a supposed criminal investigation into the killing of her 5-year-old daughter, saying that it is nothing more than a PR move meant to distract from Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza.

“Why did the investigation and the acknowledgment of the shooting at Hind’s car and at the paramedics come only after more than two years?” Wesam Hamada, Hind’s mother, told the Associated Press on Friday. “It’s an attempt to distract from what’s happening in Gaza and improve the [Israeli] army’s image to the world. That’s it.”

On Wednesday, Israel’s military acknowledged that its soldiers played a role in the horrific series of events in January 2024, in which Hind, her 15-year-old cousin, and five members of their family were killed.

The military admitted to the slaughter of her adult family members, but did not take responsibility for the killing of Hind or her cousin Layan Hamada specifically, despite numerous independent investigations finding that they were shot by Israeli soldiers in a tank. Israeli soldiers have been found to be targeting children in Gaza, often with gunshots to the head, countless other times since Hind’s killing.

“I don’t trust the Israeli authorities, I don’t trust their government, and I don’t trust any justice system they have,” Hind’s mother said in an interview with NBC. “I don’t want an investigation used to whitewash anyone’s image.”

Hind’s grandmother, who is also named Hind Rajab, similarly dismissed the investigation. “For us this is not an admission but rather an attempt by the Israeli army to justify to the world how it committed the crime and how they executed Hind,” she told AFP. “The army is trying to justify its position to the world, claiming that what happened was a mistake and that the soldiers who committed it will be prosecuted.”

An Israeli tank sprayed the car carrying Hind and her family members with hundreds of bullets, despite having a clear line of sight to the children inside, an investigation by Forensic Architecture found.

After her family was killed, Hind remained trapped in the car with their bodies for hours, a tank looming nearby, as Palestinian Red Crescent workers waited for the Israeli military to give clearance for them to rescue her. In those hours, she spoke with rescuers and her mother on the phone. Recordings from the Palestinian Red Crescent documented the terrifying last hours of the little girl’s life before she was gunned down.

“I’m so scared, please come. Please call someone to come and take me,” Hind said to emergency dispatchers.

Rajab noted that Israel only acknowledged Hind’s killing because her harrowing phone call to rescuers became so widely known, pointing out that there are many other similarly horrific killings that Israel will never follow up on.

Hind’s family still mourns her death.

“She died with the most heartbreaking sound I’ve ever heard,” Hamada told NBC. “Even now, all I hear is her crying, ‘I’m scared,’ and her plea: ‘Come here, Mama, take me.’”

Hamada has demanded an independent investigation that will actually lead to answers. “I want to know who killed my daughter, who killed my family members, and who killed the paramedics who went to rescue her. Who gave the orders? Who fired the shots?”

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Trump’s FDA Pick Raises Concerns Over Science, Abortion Access, and Food Safety
content:
On Wednesday, August 19, President Trump announced that he will nominate Dr. Heidi Overton as the new Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner. Overton’s nomination comes as the country battles a multistate cyclospora outbreak, which continues to raise serious concerns about the health and safety of the nation’s food supply.

If she is confirmed, she would succeed former FDA commissioner Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned in May 2026 after facing heavy criticism from the Trump administration and anti-abortion organizations for not restricting access to mifepristone and for his handling of drug and vaccine approvals. At a time when the FDA has come under political pressure, it is clear that the nation’s health and well-being are no longer a primary concern.

Overton is a double board-certified physician in public health and general preventive medicine. She currently serves as a senior White House health policy aide and has made no secret of her conservative stance during her tenure. In fact, Overton is a strong supporter of Trump’s health agenda, especially regarding the childhood vaccine schedule and restrictions on access to mifepristone. She also supports the false narrative that the current vaccine schedule’s timing may be a cause of rising rates of autism spectrum disorder. However, no medical evidence confirms any such link. Nevertheless, Overton has encouraged blue states to adopt these “gold standard” recommendations.

Despite Trump’s support for Overton, whom he believes is the “rockstar” and the right person to serve as the new FDA commissioner, many rightly question her qualifications to lead across the aisle. To be confirmed by the Senate, Overton must gain approval from the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

Committee Chair Sen. Bill Cassidy, an avid critic of Trump’s position on vaccines, has already expressed his disapproval of Overton. Democratic committee member Sen. Patty Murray believes that Overton is a “far-right, anti-abortion extremist who has no business leading the FDA.” Additionally, as cases of the cyclospora outbreak continue to spike, the nation still needs an experienced professional; no record shows that Overton is particularly well known for food safety issues.

Unfortunately, a recurring theme among the administration’s nominations, agency leaders, and appointees is the continued failure to equate experience with education. Although Overton is a medical professional, she does not believe in “sound science.” Instead, Overton is a medical professional willing to let partisan politics stand in the way of the nation’s health and safety.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: ‘You saved a lot of our people’: Four syilx Nation members honoured for contributions
content:
With her family, colleagues and community surrounding her, an emotional nkwancinem Kim Montgomery is gifted a special fox pelt from her sister on July 23, honouring 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


With her family, colleagues and community surrounding her, an emotional nkwancinem Kim Montgomery was gifted a special fox pelt to honour her 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance (ONA).


A key and dedicated member of ONA’s wellness team, nkwancinem was honoured by her colleagues in her home community of the Lower Similkameen Indian Band.

She was one of four syilx Nation members to have had their lifelong achievements and contributions to the community celebrated at the ONA’s 2026 annual general assembly, which took place July 22 and 23 in sməqmíx homelands.


nkwancinem Kim Montgomery, third from the left, walks with her family and community at Similkameen powwow arbour grounds on July 23, after being honoured for her 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


As the mental health lead

 for the

Okanagan Nation Response Team

, nkwancinem oversees a group of “community members who have received extensive training in the areas of suicide education, community mobilization, and critical incident response.”


“We have the skills in our communities to take care of our people,”

she told IndigiNews in 2021.


“We forget we have the timxw (wildlife), we have ceremony, we have the sweat, we have the water, we have rose bush. We have all the things we do in our grief work.”


ONA wellness team manager c̓ʔak̕ʷm Jennifer Lewis called nkwancinem her “sister” and “comrade,” and acknowledged “her love, her passion, her commitment to the people and to the future.”


“It’s really important to honour her. We would not be where we’re at,” said c̓ʔak̕ʷm.


“Twenty years, Kim. There’s some children that you’ve impacted that are young adults. You’ve impacted Elders. You’ve impacted babies. You’ve impacted fathers, mothers. All of our people.”


smukaxen Inez Pierre described nkwancinem as “a warrior woman,” adding that “there’s not many people that will walk into our communities when we’re troubling.”


“She goes into homes when we’ve lost our Elders. She goes into homes when our children are not wanting to live,” smukaxen said of nkwancinem.


“A lot of the things that you hear us talking about is what’s best for the Youth — this one can speak at that … You don’t see and find this kind of woman easily.”


The gift pays tribute to fox’s esteemed role in the syilx Nation’s collection of oral stories, teachings and histories — known as

captikʷł

 — where fox is a notable companion to sen’klip (coyote).


“sen’klip gets involved with lots of trouble and mischief. But he also made laws for our people. Fox brings coyote back to life,” said smukaxen.


She explained that in their stories, fox is always there to gather pieces of coyote and put him back together.


“And for you, Kim, you are that. You saved a lot of our people, from the babies to the Elders. The old people. You’ve done that. You’ve brought a lot of us back to life.”


An emotional nkwancinem Kim Montgomery is gifted a special fox pelt from her sister on July 23, honouring 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Similarly, nkwancinem’s sister, Tara Montgomery — the communications lead for ONA — said that her sister has dedicated her life to “breathing life back into people.”


Along with c̓ʔak̕ʷm, Tara wrapped the fox pelt around her sister’s neck. With her community behind her and her new gift, nkwancinem walked hand-in-hand with her loved ones, circling the Similkameen powwow arbour grounds before proudly dancing at its centre.


nkwancinem Kim Montgomery dances at the Similkameen powwow arbour grounds on July 23, after being honoured for her 20 years of service with the Okanagan Nation Alliance.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


The day before nkwancinem was honoured, fellow nation members Lillian Marchand, Buzz Manuel Jr., and Kelly Terbasket each had similar celebration ceremonies. 


All three were honoured with blankets, and both community members and syilx leadership lined up to greet and congratulate them each. Like nkwancinem, the community cheered them on as they circled the powwow arbour grounds with their loved ones.

author: Cory Massimino
title: Anarkisme dan Hierarki
content:
Oleh:

Cory Massimino

. “Teks aslinya berjudul “

Indi

vidualist Anarchism and Hierarchy

”. Diterjemahkan ke dalam Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa


Hubungan antara anarkisme dan hierarki memang rumit dan penuh persoalan. Sebagian anarkis menyatakan diri menentang segala bentuk hierarki, bahkan terkadang mendefinisikan anarkisme dengan cara demikian. Sebagian lainnya menyatakan bahwa mereka pada dasarnya hanya menentang negara dan tidak terlalu mempersoalkan hierarki itu sendiri. Menurut saya, anarkisme individualis, jika dipahami dengan tepat, berada di suatu titik di antara kedua ekstrem tersebut.


Singkatnya, anarkisme individualis berpandangan bahwa individu manusia adalah fondasi dari apa yang kita sebut sebagai “masyarakat”. Karena itu, sistem politik apa pun, atau lebih tepatnya sistem nonpolitik apa pun, yang diterapkan seharusnya menempatkan individu sebagai yang utama dan menghormati kedaulatannya sebagai makhluk yang bebas. Sistem non-politik yang paling mampu mewujudkan hal tersebut adalah anarkisme.


Hierarki adalah “

suatu sistem atau organisasi di mana orang atau kelompok ditempatkan dalam tingkatan yang berbeda berdasarkan status atau kewenangan

.” Dalam beberapa keadaan, sistem semacam ini pada dasarnya memang salah atau buruk. Dalam keadaan lain, hierarki dapat diterima dan bahkan baik. Ada pula keadaan di mana hierarki tidak dengan sendirinya buruk, tetapi tetap layak dipersoalkan.


Hierarki jelas menjadi problematis, bahkan tidak bermoral, ketika dipertahankan melalui inisiasi kekerasan. Sebagai kaum individualis, kami mempertahankan kedaulatan individu dan memandang otonomi pribadi seseorang sebagai sesuatu yang sangat penting secara moral. Kemampuan untuk menggunakan segenap kemampuan dan kapasitas yang dimiliki sebaik mungkin, sesuai dengan kehendaknya sendiri, merupakan hak mendasar setiap individu. Dan karena setiap orang memiliki hak tersebut, hal ini sekaligus menetapkan batas ketika seseorang secara paksa menghalangi tindakan orang lain.


Menundukkan tujuan orang lain melalui kekerasan dan menggantinya dengan tujuan kita sendiri merupakan penghinaan terhadap individualitas kedua belah pihak sekaligus pelanggaran terhadap hak. Tindakan agresi memang tidak bermoral pada dirinya sendiri. Namun sebuah sistem hierarki yang dipertahankan melalui agresi membuat individu tertentu tunduk pada kewenangan individu lainnya. Ketika seseorang tidak lebih dari seorang hamba yang harus patuh kepada tingkatan hierarki yang lebih tinggi, tidak ada lagi ruang bagi individualitas. Dan tentu saja, itulah sesuatu yang kami tentang.


Hal ini membawa kaum individualis pada penolakan terhadap penggunaan kekerasan dan, karenanya, terhadap negara. Bertentangan dengan pandangan para teoritikus kontrak sosial, negara bergantung pada kekerasan untuk mempertahankan sumber pendanaannya sekaligus monopoli atas penggunaan kekuatan yang dianggap sah di suatu wilayah. Negara merupakan sistem predator yang agresif dan hierarkis. Negara adalah antitesis dari individualisme.


Bagi banyak anarkis, kepemilikan pribadi pada dasarnya bersifat hierarkis dan karena itu tidak dapat diterima. Mereka hanya setengah benar. Dalam pengertian tertentu, kepemilikan pribadi memang menciptakan hierarki antara pemilik suatu properti dan orang lain. Namun kepemilikan pribadi juga memiliki manfaat lain yang layak dipertimbangkan. Tidak ada alasan bagi kita untuk membatasi analisis hanya pada pertanyaan apakah sesuatu menciptakan hierarki atau tidak. Ada faktor-faktor lain yang juga relevan secara moral.


Kepemilikan pribadi berguna karena berbagai alasan, dan banyak di antaranya berkaitan dengan konsekuensi yang dihasilkannya. Sistem kepemilikan pribadi menciptakan masyarakat yang makmur dan sejahtera, sekaligus memungkinkan sumber daya yang langka dialokasikan secara efisien. Selain itu, dan ini sangat penting bagi kaum individualis, kepemilikan pribadi merupakan hal yang vital bagi otonomi pribadi. Seperti ditulis Roderick Long,


“Kebutuhan manusia akan otonomi, yaitu kemampuan untuk mengendalikan hidupnya sendiri tanpa campur tangan orang lain. Tanpa kepemilikan pribadi, saya tidak memiliki tempat yang dapat saya anggap sebagai milik saya sendiri. Saya tidak memiliki ruang yang terlindungi di mana saya dapat mengambil keputusan tanpa dihambat oleh kehendak orang lain. Jika otonomi dalam pengertian ini memiliki nilai, maka kita membutuhkan kepemilikan pribadi untuk mewujudkan dan melindunginya.”


Tanpa kepemilikan pribadi, ruang …

author: Stephanie Guilloud
title: Atlanta offers a model for building sanctuary
content:
This article

Atlanta offers a model for building sanctuary

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Atlanta community organizer Bassey Etuk opened a community defense workshop this past March with a stark observation, and heads nodded around the crowded room. “Atlanta was a sanctuary city until the governor of Georgia made it illegal in 2009. Now Atlanta is Cop City,” he said. 


From California to Kenya, whenever I say I’m based in Atlanta, people immediately bring up

Cop City

, the police training facility that sparked years of protest and major campaigns to prevent it from being built on public land. The training facility was ultimately built and is now in operation. But the Stop Cop City movement reduced the size and scale of the compound and, importantly, captured the imagination of people fighting on the frontlines against policing and state violence around the world.


In 2026, organizers in Atlanta have shifted from protests and mass mobilizations to applying the lessons they learned from the campaign and building the infrastructure needed to practice real community safety every day.


I am a longtime organizer and senior strategist with Project South, where I work alongside Bassey, an Atlanta-native who organizes in the 10 historically Black neighborhoods of Brownsville in southeast Atlanta. For the past two months, Bassey, I and the ATL Get Ready Team — a coalition of community organizers and organizations from across the city — launched a community preparedness plan to respond to escalating ICE enforcement, policing and National Guard deployments in cities across the United States. Together, we have been recruiting businesses, churches, bars and community centers to become “

Sanctuary Zones

” — sites that commit to preventing ICE and other law enforcement from entering. 


Building sanctuary and protection for all people is critical in this period. It keeps us alive through moments of immediate crisis while positioning our communities to build the power needed for deeper, fundamental change. We share the lessons we are learning on the ground so that we are moving in coordination and solidarity with other communities all over the country who are similarly experiencing the trauma of this moment — the murders, detentions, intimidation and indictments — as fascist forces attempt to consolidate power at every level of society.


Atlanta gets ready


After witnessing ICE operations in Minnesota and National Guard deployments in Memphis and

Washington, D.C.

, 15 Atlanta-based organizations came together in February 2026 and asked each other some hard questions. If federal agents surge into, deploy across, or occupy Atlanta, are we ready? Are we ready to resist, to protect our communities and to prevent killings and kidnappings? Are we ready to put aside old tensions and disagreements? Are we ready to see ourselves as connected and act together, applying unified pressure in pursuit of our shared goals of community protection and collective defense?


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


At our first coalition meeting, Adelina Nicholls of the

Georgia Latino Alliance for Human Rights

 said it clearly: “We can no longer afford to mobilize in reaction to what is happening. We have to determine a political direction and alignment towards a real vision.”


Large-scale anti-ICE protests have been powerful demonstrations of collective dissent and people power. But we understood that without greater unity across race, class, gender and geography, we could not win.


It was a vital moment for those of us who have organized in Atlanta for a long time. Organizations that did not always work together and that openly acknowledged long-standing tensions and disagreements, decided that, given the rise in state repression and violence, we need each other differently in this moment.


In the face of ICE raids in Latino, Caribbean and African immigrant neighborhoods, ongoing police violence against Black youth,

sweeps

 of homeless encampments ahead of the World Cup in Atlanta, and the targeting of youth and trans people at the federal and state levels, we named criminalization as a shared reality and a political baseline for our alignment and collective action.


We agreed on a single commitment: to prevent and disrupt the growing criminalization of all our people. We called ourselves the ATL Get Ready Team, and we began by sharing trainings and building our …

author: Mike Ludwig
title: What DeFlock? Week of Action Confronts the AI Surveillance State
content:
Photo by

Paul Goyette via Flickr

.

This story was co-published with

Truthout

.


The

op-ed

 Canyen Ashworth wrote last September may have been critical of the police where he lives in Lenexa, Kansas, but it could hardly be considered radical. A

racist and nonsensical

 police investigation into the immigration status of a sitting city council member had generated embarrassing headlines, and a chaotic Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raid on a beloved local taqueria went

viral

. Pointing to basic reforms, Ashworth argued Lenexa’s city leaders had “work to do” in order to “meet the moment” and restore trust among residents.


  “It wasn’t

ACAB

. It wasn’t,

‘You guys should be hung by your ankles,’

” Ashworth told

Truthout

. “It was very much just like,

‘Lenexa, be better.’

”


  A few weeks later, a local reporter knocked on Ashworth’s door and said police were investigating him. An open records request

revealed

 that a public information officer at the Lenexa Police Department distributed a copy of his op-ed to command staff the morning it was published on September 30.


  At some point, Ashworth became the main suspect in a police investigation into a person the cops dubbed the  “Paper Hanger” — a person wearing a hoodie who was seen on surveillance footage pasting posters to a light pole four days before Ashworth’s op-ed was published. One of the posters showed a federal agent with a vest that read “Police ICE” and “Kidnapping Taskforce,” and included the words “remember when we killed fascists.” Ashworth says he did not put up the posters — he was content writing the op-ed for

The


Kansas City Star.


  “I personally thought they were pretty cool, like pictures of CEOs with devil horns,” Ashworth said. “People put up posters all the time and nobody really cares, but this particular brand of posters the city didn’t really like much.”


  On October 21, Lenexa police sent out a “be on the lookout” alert for the suspect in the Paper Hanger case — every police officer in Lenexa was told to be searching for Ashworth. “

This is MYOC,

” a Lenexa city crime analyst reportedly wrote in the alert, short for “make your own case.” In other words, the police did not have evidence tying Ashworth to a crime, so officers would have to find a reason on their own to make an arrest.


  “He doesn’t get out much; [his] last hit [was] a week ago today and appeared to come from McKeever’s,” the crime analyst wrote, referring to the grocery store Ashworth shops at regularly. “If you contact him (Ashworth) please note his shoes, as the suspect has only worn the ones pictured below.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


Sign Up


  Along with details on Ashworth’s shoes and shopping habits, the alert included a photo of his car and license plate next to a separate surveillance photo of the Paper Hanger, a black-clad figure on an apparent wheat-pasting mission. Police gathered the information with surveillance cameras that are also automated license plate readers (ALPRs).


  “They inferred, based on how much my car goes through the license plate readers, that it seems like he doesn’t get out very much,” Ashworth said with a laugh. “Which was like, super rude.”


  Often referred to as “Flock cameras,” a reference to leading manufacturer Flock Safety, ALPR systems have been around for years but are sold with increasingly advanced capabilities and software. Surveillance is

powered

 by artificial intelligence (AI), allowing police to combine data streams from multiple sources —

including advanced drones

 and cameras with

powerful zoom lenses

 that follow body movements. Flock Safety competes with companies such as Axon, Motorola Solutions, and Genetec as the market for such products

grows

 steadily thanks to tax dollars spent by law enforcement.


  The implications are serious. Ashworth said either the police read his op-ed and jumped to the conclusion that he must be the Paper Hanger — a leap of investigative logic that seems dubious at best — or they didn’t like what he had to say and made him a target for detailed surveillance with help from a network of ALPRs positioned across the town.


  At no point was Ashworth arrested; police found no evidence he was the Paper Hanger, after all. Lenexa Police Chief Eric Schmitz told local

NPR

 affiliate

KCUR

 the investigation was related to property damage, not …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Joke About Rebooting ‘Twilight’ but Bella Is Gay This Time
content:
During their press tour for their upcoming stoner buddy comedy The Wrong Girls, Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat stopped by Bravo studios for Watch What Happens Live. During the interview, Andy Cohen asks a question from a fan about Kristen saying she would reboot Twilight, and Kristen says she was mostly joking but would consider doing a continuation vs. a re-hashing of the source material. Alia Shawkat jumps in and jokes, “Bella would come back and be like ‘I’m gay,” which makes Kristen Stewart double over with laughter. Alia goes on to joke it would be “hot, modern, fresh” and they encourage Kristen’s wife Dylan Meyer to write it, and she jokes that she already has while standing in the bartender spot on the set.

Kristen Stewart goes on to joke that Bella would say, “I’m gonna fuck your whole family” and then realizes she’s never actually said that phrase before but, “God, it feels good.”

And this, friends, is why queer people should be in charge of everything.

It’s no surprise they wanted to recruit Dylan Meyer for this imaginary project, because she wrote The Wrong Girls; it’s her directorial debut, and Kristen Stewart has said she loved working with her wife. The feeling was mutual, with Dylan having only good things to say about working with Kristen. Alia Shawkat even joined in the lovefest, saying Dylan “was such a great leader, so calm and grounded and appreciative of everybody’s time and clear about what she wanted”

All in all, this trio seems like they’re on fire, so why NOT get them to reboot the Twilight series, but gayer this time. They can play vampire kickball instead of baseball this time, and it will be wonderful.

+ Sterling Point‘s Missi Pyle is cool with dating any gender, according to her conversation with King Princess on a podcast (she has played queer at least three times, including in Harlan Coben’s Shelter with Constance Zimmer, so this is not a huge surprise!)

+ Bisexual actress Inde Navarette has been cast as Rogue in the upcoming X-Men movie

+ Ariana Grande brought Cynthia Erivo on stage for two surprise duets during her London show

+ Demi Lovato returns as Mitchie in Camp Rock 3, now out on Disney+

+ Rebecca Ferguson and Greta Lee were caught filming a smooch for an upcoming mystery film

+ Queer director Ally Pankiw rejected an offer to be part of the Harry Potter series (an offer that the asker already knew her answer to) because it really is that easy to be a trans ally and put your money where your mouth is

+ Queer director Kate Herron also turned them down…twice

+ Rosie O’Donnell was on Amy Poehler’s Good Hang podcast, where she talked about her career, her nonbinary child, and what it was like filming a sex scene with her good friend Cynthia Nixon

+ The TV show Monster will feature Lizzie Borden as its fourth season’s main character

+ People are already shipping Elsa with the female villain in Frozen 3 and they haven’t even seen her yet (I’m very team “give Elsa a girlfriend or leave her single”)

+ Hayden Panettiere, who recently came out as bisexual via her memoir, has sadly passed away

author: Leanne Sanders
title: First Nations leaders reflect as they commemorate the signing of Treaty 6
content:
First Nations from across Treaty 6 territory are celebrating and in Saskatchewan, will commemorate 150 years since the signing of the historic Treaty document.


Treaty 6 spans a wide swath of what is now northern Alberta and Saskatchewan.


It was signed on Aug. 23, 1876, at Fort Carlton and Sept. 9 at Fort Pitt. There were later adhesions to the Treaty through 1950.


Negotiated between the British Crown and Cree, Nakota (Assiniboine), Saulteaux, and Dene leaders, it covers central portions of present-day Alberta and Saskatchewan. It was intended to share the land in exchange for vital guarantees and meant to last “as long as the sun shines, the grass grows, and the river flows.”


Events are scheduled across the territory over the coming weekend-one of the largest being the Treaty 6 Commemoration at Fort Carlton, 100 kilometres north of Saskatoon by highway. The original Treaty parchment that was signed is available for viewing through Saturday.


First Nations leaders and Indigenous commentators have been weighing in about the importance of the Treaty and its anniversary.


“Today we honour our ancestors who stood together and entered into Treaty with hope for the generations yet to come,” said James Smith Cree Nation Chief Kirby Constant in a Facebook post while also calling on Canada to remember the promises that were made.


“We remember their strength, their sacrifices, and the promises that were made. A century and a half later, we are still here, still strong, still carrying our language, culture, ceremonies and our inherent rights forward. We honour the Treaty, we honour our ancestors, and we continue the work until every promise is fulfilled. We ask Canada to do the same.”


Another post by John Brady McDonald, a Nehiyawak-Metis writer and artist with ties to Muskeg Lake Cree Nation said the anniversary is an emotional one.


“Chief Mistawasis is my great great great grandfather. I am a direct descendant, as my great grandfather, Chief George Dreaver, was his grandson.


“150 years ago this weekend, Chief Mistawasis was the first signatory to Treaty Six at Fort Carlton.150 years ago, he made a decision he felt was the best for the survival of his family and those of his band. I will forever be proud of him, for he set the example of thinking of the survival of others,” McDonald said.


He shared a quote from a speech by Chief Mistawasis the day the Treaty was signed.


“I have heard my brothers speak, complaining of the hardships endured by our people. Some have bewailed the poverty and suffering that has come to Indians because of the destruction of the buffalo as the chief source of our living, the loss of the ancient glory of our forefathers; and with all that I agree, in the silence of my teepee and on the broad prairies where once our fathers could not pass for the great number of those animals that blocked their way; and even in our day, we have had to choose carefully our campground for fear of being trampled in our teepees,” Mistawasis said.


“With all these things, I think and feel intensely the sorrow my brothers express.


I speak directly to Poundmaker and The Badger and those others who object to signing this treaty. Have you anything better to offer our people? I ask, again, can you suggest any-thing that will bring these things back for tomorrow and all the tomorrows that face our people? I for one think that the Great White Queen Mother has offered us a way of life when the buffalo are no more. Gone they will be before many snows have come to cover our heads or graves if such should be,” his speech concluded.


“What we speak of and do now will last as long as the sun shines and the river runs, we are looking forward to our children’s children, for we are old and have but few days to live,” said a signatory at Fort Pitt, Sept. 9, 1876, Chief Weekaskookwasayin, or Chief Sweet Grass Abraham Wikaskokiseyin.


The Confederacy of Treaty 6 First Nations, headquartered in Alberta said “150 years later, we are still here.”


”Still gathering. Still dancing. Still singing our songs. Still carrying our languages, our ceremonies, our teachings and our responsibilities to Treaty,”said Grand Chief Joey Pete.


“This week was more than a commemoration of history. It was a reminder that Treaty No. 6 is not something of the past. Treaty is living. Treaty is forever.”
