author: Carissa Lee
title: MEDIA STATEMENT : FELIPE ALVAREZ CORONIAL INQUEST
content:
FELIPE ALVAREZ: FAMILY CALLS FOR ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND CORONIAL REFORM AFTER ACT CORONER’S FINDINGS


By Gabriela Alvarez-Sledge

Sister of the late Felipe Esteban Alvarez


Disclaimer: Readers please be advised this article mentions someone who has passed away.


“Felipe’s life mattered. His death mattered. What we learn from his death matters.”


The family of the late

Felipe Esteban Alvarez

 is calling for greater transparency, accountability and reform of the ACT coronial system following the release of the findings into his death.


Felipe died in March 2021 following an overdose at his Canberra residence.


Five years later, his family is still grieving while asking an important question:


What can be changed so that another family does not have to go through what ours has experienced?


Felipe was not simply a coronial file.


He was a brother, son, uncle and deeply loved member of his family.


His life had value.


His family believes his death deserved to be investigated as thoroughly, transparently and independently as possible.


WHAT THE CORONER FOUND


The findings of ACT Coroner Ken Archer identified serious concerns surrounding the circumstances of Felipe’s death.


The Coroner found that Felipe was experiencing a medical emergency and that emergency medical assistance was not sought for a significant period of time.


The Coroner found that the delay deprived Felipe of any chance of survival he may have had following his initial collapse.


The Coroner described the conduct of those present as

“morally blameworthy”

 and found that their conduct demonstrated a serious indifference to the possibility of loss of life.


The findings also identified broader public-safety concerns relating to the Canberra Alliance for Harm Minimisation and Advocacy (CAHMA), including concerns about governance, recruitment and screening, overdose-response training, naloxone availability and organisational accountability.


The Coroner found that appropriate screening and eligibility processes should have been applied to the relevant peer workers.


The findings also raised concerns about the organisation’s response following Felipe’s death and the need for stronger governance and accountability.


The Coroner recommended improvements to overdose-response training and stronger collaboration between harm-minimisation services, health agencies, ambulance services and police.


The family welcomes those recommendations.


THE FAMILY’S CONCERNS REMAIN


Throughout the coronial process, Felipe’s family provided information, documents and concerns about matters they believed were important to understanding what happened.


The family identified people who were present when Felipe suffered his overdose and sought to have the relevant evidence properly considered.


The family also provided written material that it believed was relevant to understanding what occurred.


However, the family remained concerned that not every matter it believed was important was fully tested or explored during the coronial process.


Because the Court has imposed restrictions concerning the publication of identities,

the family will not identify any person whose identity is subject to suppression

.


The family respects the Court’s orders.


There will be no naming of suppressed individuals in this statement.


The family’s concern has never been about publicly naming people.


It is about evidence.


It is about transparency.


It is about whether families can have confidence that every reasonable avenue of inquiry has been considered when their loved one dies.


THIS IS NOT AN ATTACK ON THE CORONER


The family wishes to make this position very clear.


Gabriela   Alvarez-Sledge is not seeking to undermine the independence of the Coroner or interfere with the findings.


She acknowledges the Coroner’s findings and welcomes the public-safety recommendations.


The family’s concern is about what can be learned from the entire experience.


A coronial system should not only determine how a person died.


It should also give bereaved families confidence that the investigation was thorough, transparent, fair and independent.


Where families continue to have genuine concerns about aspects of a coronial process, there should be an appropriate and independent pathway for those concerns to be considered.


A CALL FOR CORONIAL REFORM

author: AWSM
title: A Community in the Cracks of Capitalism
content:
A piece of Christchurch that the property market abandoned after the earthquakes has become home to people abandoned by the property market. The old Bexley neighbourhood was largely cleared after liquefaction made conventional residential development impossible. Houses disappeared, streets remained and the land sat waiting for whatever official purpose would eventually be found for it. Into that gap came people who needed somewhere to live. They arrived in cars, vans, buses and tents. Some were working. Some were retired. Some had children. They did what people have always done when the institutions around them fail, they improvised. A community grew. Earlier this year about 40 people were living around Wetlands Grove; reports now put the number at more than 100. Christchurch City Council has told them they must leave by 28 February 2027 because the area is intended for wetland development. There is an obvious temptation to treat this as a story about homelessness, council planning or the difficulties of finding somewhere suitable for a group of people living in vehicles. It is all of those things, but underneath them sits a much simpler question. What is land for? The answer given by our economic system is that land belongs to whoever has legal title to it, and its legitimate use is determined by owners, planners and institutions. The people actually living on it remain secondary. They may sleep there, look after one another there and make the place usable through their own effort, but none of that gives them any meaningful claim to it. Their relationship to the place exists only for as long as the legal owner tolerates it. That distinction between ownership and use lies close to the heart of the anarchist criticism of private property.

The people living at Wetlands Grove have already demonstrated something that governments spend enormous amounts of money trying unsuccessfully to manufacture through policy documents – people can organise social life themselves. Earlier reporting described an informal community growing around buses, vans and cars, with neighbours helping one another through winter and a communal tent being established as shared space. One man who had been sleeping in a small tent was helped into an old car when the cold became severe. Council rubbish collection and portable toilets made conditions more bearable, but the social organisation of the place came largely from the people living there. Moko, one of the informal figures in the community, was working full-time on an on-call road crew. Others were pensioners. Ngawai Timu described abandoning a $470-a-week rental because she felt she was spending her life paying somebody else’s mortgage. Polly Stewart was surviving on the pension in a bus. Families were living there too, including a woman with several children living from a bus. These details matter because homelessness is constantly spoken about as though it were primarily a pathology of homeless people. Addiction, mental illness, poor budgeting, antisocial behaviour and bad choices are summoned as explanations because those explanations leave the social order intact. They allow us to imagine that housed people possess some quality that homeless people lack. Wetlands Grove makes that story harder to sustain. When people with jobs cannot obtain housing, when pensioners decide rent leaves too little for ordinary life, and when families find themselves competing with dozens of others for a private rental, the problem is no longer plausibly located inside the individual. There are certainly people living rough who struggle with addiction or serious psychological distress. There are also people who get up and go to work from a tent. A housing system that cannot reliably house either has failed at the most elementary level.

New Zealand has become remarkably skilled at describing this failure without challenging the institution producing it. We talk about housing supply, affordability pressures and housing need. We devise eligibility categories and waiting lists. We construct administrative pathways through emergency housing, transitional housing, community housing and social housing. Every stage acquires its own assessments and rules. The language becomes more sophisticated while people remain without homes. author: James McVicar
title: Students teach Hanson a lesson
content:
Across the country yesterday, students walked out of their schoolrooms and lecture halls and flooded into the streets to protest against Pauline Hanson and her far-right political project.

As many as 4,000 marched in Sydney. Two thousand in Perth and Adelaide and 1,000 in Brisbane. In Canberra, 500 students protested at the Australian National University campus and 200 turned out in Wollongong. High schoolers spontaneously organised protests in Shoalhaven, Lismore, and Albury. In Melbourne, where I was, the march was colossal—about 5,000 people—and the mood was absolutely electric.

The chants rang out with righteous rage: “Too young to protest? We call bullshit!” and “High school, uni, teachers too; Pauline Hanson, we’re coming for you!” Undoubtedly the most popular was a two-word refrain: “Fuck Pauline!” Sometimes less is more.

The homemade placards were funny and indignant and withering. “I love naps but I stay woke”. “Still got a better attendance rate than Hanson”. “Orange is the new evil”. On the ground I spotted a papier-mache Hanson head that, from the looks of it, had had a run-in with a few too many shiny black shoes.

Anyone over the age of 25 knows what it’s like to be roasted by teenagers. Gen Z sarcasm is one of the most devastating weapons humankind has ever known. So just try to imagine how Hanson must be feeling right now.

All she could muster as a response was a post on X: “If you want to protest something, protest why your parents’ wages are going backwards and the cost of everything is going up ... Whether you know it or not, One Nation and I are fighting for you”. Please don’t hurt me, kids, I’m actually on your side! Pathetic.

The students were protesting against the increasing entrenchment of far-right politics in Australia being spearheaded by Hanson and One Nation. It’s clear to them that Hanson’s reactionary agenda only serves the big end of town. It’s not just Gina Rinehart: more and more wealthy backers are swinging in behind One Nation.

Hanson’s project to demonise migrants and attack the rights of women and workers helps to prop up a society where the few rule over the many. Odessa, a High School Anti-Capitalists member from Huntingtower, hit the nail on the head in her speech: “We know she’s a servant for the wealthy”.

At the same time, the mainstream parties have ceded more and more ground to One Nation. The Liberals are doing their level best to rebrand as One Nation in neckties. Labor politicians are planning to announce substantial cuts to migration. They too want to run a system based on extreme wealth inequality, hard borders and minority rule, so we cannot count on them to stand up to the far right.

One Nation’s rise is part of a broader global shift in politics. Aero, an international student at RMIT and member of Socialist Alternative, spoke about President Javier Milei in Argentina, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Italy, Nigel Farage in the UK and Donald Trump in America. Students know what’s going on abroad and know it needs to be fought. “Australia does not need our own orange clown”, read one placard.

Around the world, capitalism has less and less to offer people but wage cuts and declining living standards. As governments pour more and more money into war preparations, welfare and social spending are being slashed. The far-right’s authoritarian politics, their championing of social hierarchy and oppression—it all fits the bill for our rulers.

In the middle of the State Library forecourt, the haughty statue of Supreme Court judge and first chancellor of Melbourne University Redmond Barry became a rostrum for unruly teens calling out “Pauline Hanson is a fascist!” Old Redmond would have had a fit. The other two statues outside the State Library—St George slaying a dragon on one side and a triumphant Joan of Arc on the other—seemed a little more the vibe of the day.

This was a protest of students from schools and universities across the country, but the high schoolers were the heroes of the day. I spoke to students from Melbourne High who reckoned there were 40 of them marching. Another 50 from both Northcote High and Coburg High. There were thousands more, including students from as far away as Geelong, Ballarat and Bendigo. Sixty schools were represented at the Sydney rally. In Perth, rally organisers say students from 120 different schools contacted them about joining the strike.

Plenty of high schoolers had to fight for their right to even be there in the …

author: Ben Radford
title: Socialist Alliance candidates to contest Lutruwita council elections
content:
Candidates for Lutruwita Socialist Alliance (LSA) are running in three local government areas in the Lutruwita/Tasmania council elections over September to October.

Snowgum Ries is running in the Huon Valley, Matt Haubrick in Glenorchy and Sam Campbell in Hobart.

They have decided on five “core planks”, three of which they share — affordable housing, more public transport and democracy — and two community-specific planks, formulated from conversations with their communities.

While the electoral system frames all candidates as individuals rather than parties, Campbell told Green Left: “Everyone knows who belongs to what because branding, or at least colour schemes, make it pretty clear.

Campbell said his campaign is focused on making Hobart a “people-focused CBD”, including with fair rates. “It’s about prioritising human connection. This can, in part, be achieved by increasing walkability, expanding free third spaces and cultivating social spontaneity.

“I’m campaigning for streets to be recuperated from cars for the people. We could then re-green them with local native plants, while adding accessible seating, more shade and spaces for pop-up culture, like youth art, social enterprise stalls and community theatre. This is already being done multiple times a year already, so let’s just make it permanent.”

Campbell said a fairer rate system would be based on the use of, and relationship to, the local community. “For example, a residential super-landlord with multiple Short Stay Accommodations (SSAs are like Airbnbs) should pay more, not only for operating grey-hotels, but to compensate for the social costs to the surrounding community.

“Another example could be a commercial premises that lies empty for 90 or more sequential days; the landlord should pay more for not lowering rents or allowing its use for a social benefit, such as a free pop-up art space.

“Pensioners, who may own their homes, but are still struggling with the cost of living should also only have to pay lower rates. Those who can pay more, such as self-funded retirees and those with financial trusts, should pay more.”

Campbell is keen on council promoting “more mixed-use passive-haus developments”, where “a percentage must be guaranteed public homes. With differential rates, it would go a significant way towards improving affordability locally.

“Questions over planning, insurance, licenses and the cost of materials are not insurmountable. For example, council could give automatic approval for developments that meet, or exceed, pre-defined criteria, such as the use of materials like hempcrete, or structures of mass-timber like dowel-laminated (reclaimed, ethical) timber.”

Lester Ries, known as “Snowgum”, has lived and worked in the Huon Valley for their entire life. “That means I’ve seen the harsh conditions that people face and I’ve seen the optimistic grit that comes from it,” they told GL.

“People in the Huon Valley are being hit with housing unaffordability, a lack of infrastructure and healthcare facilities and severe food insecurity. This leads to a dwindling sense of community, which disproportionately affects young people and minority groups.

“Capitalism puts profits ahead of people’s needs and is the root cause of these crises.

“LSA supports setting up ‘People’s voice councils’, where decisions would then inform council policy and community land trusts, which would allow more people access to land.

“We also support a large-scale, non-commercial food security network, which could reliably supply people with the essentials.

“We are also campaigning for greater council transparency and accountability, including by council publishing its accounts and minutes and recording meetings.”

Snowgum, who is 19 years old, said young people are “disproportionately affected by cuts to services and the lack of affordable housing”. While many are sceptical about young councillors, they said young people who are passionate about listening to everyday people’s voices would make the best representatives.

“Councils are supposed to be where people’s voices are heard,” Snowgum said. “Becoming a councillor is also a good way to build support for socialist ideas and solutions to improve people’s everyday lives.”

Haubrick told GL he is campaigning to make the Glenorchy Pool community owned and operated. Given the housing shortages, he said empty homes need to be filled and public transport needs to be improved with better lighting and accessibility.

author: Luca Tavan
title: Rebel teachers taking their campaign against the Labor government all the way to parliament
content:
“I’m a rebel teacher running against Ben Carroll in Niddrie because I think workers should run the world. I think teachers know how to run schools, and we should be empowered to run the education system ... On the issue of education, the ALP is not just out of touch: they’re on the other side of the picket line, with the Liberals and One Nation.”

This is how Brendan Laws announced the Victorian “rebel educator” campaign—a group of teachers and education support staff targeting sitting Labor MPs, including Premier and former Minister for Education Ben Carroll. 

The eight candidates, all members of Victorian Socialists and the Socialists in Schools union group, have played a role in leading the rank-and-file rebellion in the Australian Education Union (AEU) Victorian Branch that has organised two massive strike days, stared down the state government and fought tooth and nail against the conservative leadership of their own union. The teachers’ fight is the most significant industrial dispute in Victoria in years, with teachers holding the line for a decent contract in the context of falling real wages and deteriorating working conditions. For many on the left, the obstinacy of Victorian Labor in the face of teachers’ demands for decent pay and tolerable working conditions embodies everything wrong with a government which once boasted of running “the most progressive state in the nation”.

Labor has governed Victoria practically uninterrupted for more than two decades, leaning heavily on the support of union members to win successive elections. AEU members were a central part of the mobilisation of 2,200 unionists who doorknocked and phone-banked to hand Daniel Andrews a surprise victory in 2014. 

Twelve years on, Victoria has the lowest-funded public schools in the country. The government has stolen $16 billion from the system through underfunding in the last seven years alone. Surging workloads, wage suppression and increasing class sizes have created a situation in which less than a third of teachers plan to stay in the sector long-term. 

Leading teacher unionist and Victorian Socialists candidate for Niddrie Brendan Laws says:

“The school I’m working at right now is relatively well resourced, but the sheer amount of work and stress is overwhelming. You’re writing and rewriting assessments, you’re marking, trying to give individual feedback. There’s this pressure, because the school is competing with over-funded private schools ... I was at a very low-income school in Werribee; you could see all the traps that students get pulled into, not having the resources to read and learn, at the same time as [Labor] were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on a nearby youth prison. You would just see the kids that were getting pulled out of school into that constantly. Eight teachers quit from my department during one school year so there weren’t enough staff and everybody else had to pull in just to fill in the gaps.”

The AEU leadership’s close-knit relationship with the Labor government means many educators feel the officials have worked against members’ interests. Workers went backwards after their 2022 contract negotiation, when the AEU leadership rushed through a sell-out deal cutting real wages by 11 percent. Forty percent of AEU members voted against the offer, at the time a historically unprecedented rejection of a leadership decision in the union. While many left the union in disgust, others waited, and pledged that next time around it would be different  

Brendan was one of around a dozen Victorian Socialists members who decided to launch Socialists in Schools in mid-2025. “The biggest indicator that there was an audience for it was how many AEU members were already part of Victorian Socialists”, he says. “We took a survey and found we had almost 100 teacher members, so it just showed that there was already a base to work with.” 

The campaign started with the modest aim of giving socialist teachers a chance to get together and chat:

“The first part was just meeting up and discussing socialist politics with the people in our campaign. It was the political arguments around militarism, the genocide in Palestine, the Labor government’s austerity and privatisation. Then when we knew that our last agreement was going to expire and the opportunity to have industrial action was going to be there, we really shifted a lot of our propaganda to educate people about striking. It had been 13 years since a strike had …

author: Nick Reich
title: Introducing the conveners of the Australian Socialist Party: Omar Hassan and Rebecca Barrigos
content:
Over the weekend of 18 July, the Australian Socialist Party was founded. Fledgling as it is, we set ourselves the task of ending an increasingly harsh capitalist system and defeating all the parties who defend that system, from One Nation to the ALP. Achieving that will involve recruiting thousands of socialists to the party, and developing them into activists who can channel the rage of working people into a real force that can win against the odds. 

The Socialist Party’s orientation to its members is unlike any other on the Australian political landscape, where party leaders generally see their members as how-to-vote distribution machines or empty numbers in a faction fight. Socialists aren’t just cheerleaders for parliamentary leaders—our members are fighters. So to help build an active party membership, the Socialist Party founding conference elected two national conveners: Rebecca Barrigos and Omar Hassan.

Both Barrigos and Hassan are teachers and union activists, both have been members of Socialist Alternative since the mid-2000s, both have led impressive campaigns in their home states over the past 20 years, and they’ve each played leading roles in establishing Queensland Socialists and Victorian Socialists respectively. 

Speaking to

Red Flag

, Barrigos remembered the issues that spurred her to join the socialist movement as a uni student:

“The barbarism of the ‘war on terror’, the mass death toll and carnage that was unleashed on the civilian populations of Afghanistan and Iraq, the disgraceful rise of Islamophobia, racism used to justify war crimes, and attacks on civil liberties in the West to quell anti-war opposition, convinced me that I needed to join a socialist organisation that was committed to fighting every institution of the capitalist state.”

Similarly, Hassan related that he “became a socialist in the dark days of the John Howard years, furious at the racism and war that characterised that era”. 

With the resurgence of Hanson’s One Nation and the genocidal wars grinding on in the Middle East, there’s a familiarity to the rage which drove Barrigos and Hassan towards socialism in their youth. The more things change, the more they stay the same.

Sticking it out as socialist activists for two decades, in often difficult circumstances, is an admirable achievement in its own right, but those years meant more than just stubborn principles and passing time for Barrigos and Hassan. They’ve drawn lessons and inspiration from their years of organising. Hassan said that his time on the left has taught him “to appreciate the moments where working-class people come together to fight and win against the system: be it on a small picket line in suburban Melbourne or in mass protests against genocide and imperialism”. 

But mass movements have risen and declined, ebbed and flowed, sometimes scoring small victories but often leaving the fundamental injustice in place. The transience of moments when workers feel their power taught Hassan “how important it is to build a political organisation that can sustain and consolidate the lessons and experiences of those times to build a force that can translate momentum into actual victories”. 

Barrigos made a similar point when speaking about the movement against the Iraq War: “The Iraq War provoked unprecedented resistance. Millions around the world, in Europe, and here in Australia took to the streets in mobilisations even larger than the anti-Vietnam War moratoriums of the 1970s. But despite the size of these rallies, mass protests were never on their own going to stop the US war machine. If we want to win decisively, we need to build a socialist movement that mobilises the power of workers to successfully resist capitalism, and in that fight, lay the basis for a whole different society based on human need, not profit”.

Through their failures and limitations, movements of the past can give their participants a deeper understanding of what’s necessary to win. Not just a firmer conviction, but the right set of politics. Barrigos and Hassan are two among hundreds of experienced socialists who act as conveyor belts for these lessons to a new generation of radicalising young people. There are a few ways they have already been playing this role. They’ve both written insightful theoretical articles for the

Marxist Left Review

 on topics like higher education, the Middle East and Australian politics. They both give impressive speeches.

Earlier this year, Hassan …

author: Susan Price
title: Colombia: New president criticised over earthquake response
content:
Just three days after Colombia’s new president, Abelardo De la Espriella, was sworn into office, an earthquake measuring 7.4 on the Richter scale struck the western part of the country. The quake was felt particularly strongly in the regions of Chocó, Caldás, Risaralda and Valle del Cauca, among others, and was so powerful that it was even felt in neighbouring Panama and Ecuador.

So far, authorities have reported the deaths of 280 people, a figure that is rising steadily as the hours pass, especially considering that anywhere between 2,000 and 4,200 people are currently reported missing (the total number of missing varies according to different entities). In addition, more than 1,300 people have been injured, some seriously.

Hundreds of rescue workers and civilian volunteers are conducting search operations in the hope of finding survivors amid the collapsed buildings, which number more than 100 according to the latest reports.

The earthquake has become a focal point of De la Espriella’s early days as president. The new head of state was inaugurated on August 7 at a private university (breaking with protocol). Immediately after, he traveled by helicopter to a military battalion, where he delivered his first speech, sending a clear message about the future of his term: the private sector and the military, as hinted at by his military salute and his preference for private capital.

In fact, just a few hours after taking office, the Colombian government announced that several members of irregular armed groups had been killed in clashes with the armed forces, thus marking the beginning of a radical shift in the Army’s military operations. This shift is in line with De la Espriella’s promises. Throughout the campaign, he harshly criticised the peace process initiated by the government of Juan Manuel Santos and continued and strengthened by Gustavo Petro. “The option of dialogue has been completely exhausted,” said the new president.

He added: “Security is not built through concessions to crime, but through authority and perseverance … I reaffirm my intention to relentlessly defeat narco-terrorism and all criminal organisations that threaten Colombia’s freedom … El Tigre has arrived, and they will learn just how hard he bites when it comes to defending the Colombian people.”

Furthermore, the inauguration had a clear religious component, during which, amid prayers and hymns, a rabbi delivered a speech, exclaiming “Long live Israel!” to applause, thereby symbolically bringing to a close the diplomatic rift that had existed between the Colombian government and Tel Aviv during Petro’s presidency regarding Gaza. De la Espriella has stated on several occasions that he recognises the Jewish people as “God’s chosen people.”

However, his response to the earthquake has quickly overshadowed various other actions in the first days of his term.

Despite the magnitude of the tragedy, the De la Espriella administration reportedly rejected international aid that could have provided relief to the exhausted rescue workers. In fact, several countries and international organizations offered assistance to the newly elected government to help it address the crisis.

However, De la Espriella reportedly decided to disregard these offers, with the exception of the one from the United States. One of the international representatives who made this claim was the right-wing Salvadoran president, Nayib Bukele, an ally of De la Espriella: “The Colombian government has requested humanitarian aid solely in the form of supplies to assist families affected by the earthquake. We have been informed that their rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are deployed and addressing the situation; therefore, at this time, they do not require personnel support.”

Similarly, the Chinese ambassador to Colombia, Zhu Jingyang, implied on X that offers of aid were not being heeded: “We hope the Colombian government will immediately release the name of the official and their designated contact person to coordinate international assistance for the earthquake victims. Please help us spread this message — it’s urgent!”

The specific reasons for rejecting the aid are not yet known, although it has been said that the government believes it can handle the disaster on its own; others, however, have interpreted the move as a rejection of multilateralism or simply an attempt by the new government to avoid appearing weak so early in its term …

title: Eğitim Sen’den MEB genelgesine tepki: Eğitim tek tipleştiriliyor
content:
Milli Eğitim Bakanlığı'nın (MEB) 19 Ağustos'ta yayımladığı 2026/70 sayılı "2026-2027 Eğitim ve Öğretim Yılına İlişkin İş ve İşlemler" Genelgesi'ne Eğitim ve Bilim Emekçileri Sendikası'ndan (Eğitim Sen) tepki geldi.


Eğitim Sen, genelgenin "eğitimin kamusal, bilimsel, laik, çoğulcu ve demokratik niteliğini güçlendirmekten uzak" olduğunu belirterek, düzenlemelerin eğitim süreçlerini daha fazla merkezileştirdiğini ve öğretmenlerin mesleki özerkliğini sınırlandırdığını savundu.


Maarif Modeli eleştirisi


Açıklamada, Türkiye Yüzyılı Maarif Modeli'nin yalnızca öğretim programlarıyla sınırlı tutulmadığı; öğretmenlerin mesleki eğitiminden sosyal etkinliklere, okul dışı öğrenmeden dijital platformlara ve seçmeli derslere kadar okul yaşamının farklı alanlarına yayıldığı belirtildi.


Öğretmenlerin Öğretmen Bilişim Ağı (ÖBA) üzerinden hazırlanan Maarif Modeli eğitim paketlerinin tüm modüllerini tamamlamalarının istenmesine de tepki gösteren sendika, mesleki gelişimin Bakanlık politikalarının "tek yönlü aktarımı" şeklinde değil, öğretmenlerin ihtiyaçları ve bilimsel gelişmeler doğrultusunda, eğitim emekçilerinin katılımıyla planlanması gerektiğini söyledi.


MEB’den Ermeni okullarına “misafir öğrenci” denetimi


14 Ağustos 2026


"Çoğulculuk eğitim sisteminde yer almalı"


Genelgedeki "Köklerden Geleceğe" yaklaşımına da değinen Eğitim Sen, Türk dünyası ve "gönül coğrafyası" üzerinden ortak tarih, kültür ve medeniyet birikiminin öğrencilere benimsetilmesinin istendiğini aktardı.


Sendika, çocukların farklı tarih ve kültürleri öğrenmesinin değerli olduğunu ancak bunların belirli bir kültürel kimlik ve siyasal perspektifle sunulmasına itiraz etti.


Türkiye'nin çok dilli, çok kültürlü ve çok kimlikli toplumsal yapısına dikkat çeken Eğitim Sen; Kürtçe, Arapça, Ermenice, Rumca, Gürcüce, Lazca, Çerkes dilleri ve diğer halkların dil, kültür ve tarihlerinin çoğulcu bir eğitim anlayışı içinde yer almasını ve çocukların anadilinde eğitim hakkının güvence altına alınmasını istedi.


Bakanlığın haber platformuna eleştiri


Eğitim Sen'in eleştirdiği başlıklardan biri de medya okuryazarlığı oldu.


Sendika, genelgede öğrencilerin eleştirel düşünme ve medya okuryazarlığı becerilerinin geliştirilmesinden söz edilirken Bakanlığın hazırladığı "Haberimiz Olsun" platformundaki içeriklerin derslerde kullanılmasının öngörülmesini çelişkili buldu.


Medya okuryazarlığının Bakanlığın belirlediği haberlerin öğrencilere aktarılması anlamına gelmediğini belirten sendika, öğrencilerin farklı haber kaynaklarını karşılaştırabilmesi, kaynakları sorgulayabilmesi ve propaganda ile manipülasyon yöntemlerini tanıyabilmesi gerektiğini ifade etti.


MEB yönetmeliği değişti: Okul yönetimlerine arama yetkisi verildi


29 Temmuz 2026


Önlük uygulaması: "Mesleğin saygınlığı kıyafetle sağlanmaz"


Açıklamada öğretmenlerin önlük giymesinin istenmesi ve uygulamanın milli eğitim müdürlükleri tarafından takip edilecek olması da eleştirildi.


Eğitim Sen, öğretmenlik mesleğinin saygınlığının kıyafetle değil; öğretmene verilen toplumsal değer, ekonomik ve özlük hakları, mesleki özerklik ve demokratik çalışma koşullarıyla sağlanabileceğini belirtti.


Norm fazlası öğretmenler


Genelgede norm kadro fazlası öğretmenlerin herhangi bir takvime bağlı olmadan ihtiyaç bulunan eğitim kurumlarına atanması, kendisine ders görevi verilemeyen öğretmenlerin ise Milli Eğitim Akademisi'nde eğitime alınarak öğretmen ihtiyacı bulunan "diğer alanlarda" görevlendirilmesi öngörülüyor.


Eğitim Sen, bu düzenlemenin öğretmenlerin eğitim aldıkları branşların dışında görevlendirilmelerinin önünü açabileceğini savundu. Öğretmen açığının farklı branşlarda görevlendirmelerle değil, ihtiyaç bulunan alanlara yeterli sayıda kadrolu öğretmen atanarak giderilmesi gerektiğini belirtti.


Sendika ayrıca norm fazlası sorununun yanlış norm planlaması, değiştirilen ders çizelgeleri, okul dönüşümleri ve Bakanlığın istihdam politikalarıyla bağlantılı olduğunu ifade etti. 


Dijital platformlar ve öğrenci verileri


Açıklamada Yeni EBA, MEBİ, OGM Materyal, HEMBA, Velivizyon ve yapay zekâ destekli DİLİM gibi Bakanlık platformlarının yaygınlaştırılması da değerlendirildi.

author: Alexandra Bradbury
title: New Voices Gain Ground at Letter Carriers Convention
content:
“The number one takeaway is that the times in the NALC, they are a-changing,” said Margo O’Neill of Branch 352 in Des Moines, Iowa, who attended her first Letter Carriers convention August 3-7 in Los Angeles.


“It was quite different than any convention that I’ve been to,” said retiree activist Jamie Partridge of Branch 82 in Portland, Oregon, who has been attending since 1988. “There were many competing factions and five times as many constitutional amendments as have been offered in the past, and many more resolutions, which I attribute to the uprising against the current leadership.”


President Brian Renfroe was already in hot water at the last convention. He had been negotiating in such secrecy that even the rest of the executive council was kept in the dark; when he took a months-long leave for alcoholism treatment, he left no bargaining notes.


But discontent really boiled over afterwards, when Renfroe came out with a tentative deal. Members were furious at the

low raises

 and continued two-tier, and voted it down; Renfroe agreed to most of it anyway and rushed the economic parts into arbitration, citing Trump’s attacks. A

near-identical contract

 was imposed.


The union will elect a new president this fall, from a field of four candidates. After months of speculation, Renfroe announced at the convention that he isn’t running again. Delegates cheered.


“I think that eased a lot of people’s minds, and also helped sharpen the dialogue about how this isn’t just about Renfroe,” said John Murphy of Branch 4716 in Naples, Florida. “We’ve gotta move forward, get some checks and balances. The younger members want their voices to be heard. They want more transparency, they want more democracy, they want more say.”


“We’re clearly rapidly expanding what democracy looks like in our union,” said Derek Liemohn of Branch 34 in Boston. “It would be a stretch to call this a winning convention for the reformers. But this was, I think, the strongest that independent reform politics has ever looked” in the NALC.


HOMELESS IN SEATTLE


The latest contract expired in May, and the union and management went through a required mediation period this summer. Interest arbitration is expected next, but delegates didn’t get any update on the proposals or timeline.


In the week’s biggest surprise, convention delegates bucked the executive council’s recommendation and approved (1,909 to 1,781) a resolution committing the union to lobbying for a wage boost in areas with a higher cost of living, like federal workers get.


“We had old guys coming up to us and saying they had been trying to get this passed since the 1980s,” said C Moline of Branch 79 in Seattle. “This was a huge win that none of us expected this go-round.”


Letter carrier pay is tiered by hire date and job type, but not by location. The union’s longstanding position is that bargaining a local differential would pit the interests of some carriers against others.


However, carriers in Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico already get a “Territorial COLA” allocated by Congress. The resolution calls for locality pay within the continental U.S. to be accomplished the same way.


“Some of our carriers have ended up homeless because they can’t afford rent in Seattle,” Moline said in an impassioned

speech

 on the convention floor, drawing applause. “This is the way we can do it and not use any of our bargaining power. This is legislative.”


PARTICIPATION OVERLOAD


Some proposed constitutional amendments were clearly inspired by the recent contract debacle, such as requiring the president to keep the executive council briefed on bargaining progress, and preventing the union from making a deal without a member vote.


Resolutions ran the gamut from contract demands, like $30-an-hour starting pay and an end to two-tier, to political positions, like opposing the war with Iran.


Most of these efforts failed, but some modest reforms did pass. Future union conventions will be livestreamed, as this one was. The president will be required to keep written records of bargaining proposals.


Under NALC rules, any resolution or constitutional amendment submitted in time by a branch (the union’s equivalent of a local) or state association was heard by the 5,000 delegates.


Proposals where the executive council recommended a “yes” were batched together. Those the council opposed were taken one by one, in a confusing process where delegates would have to vote “no” on the council …

author: Amy Goodman
title: AI Is Only Possible Because of Global South Workers in “Digital Sweatshops”
content:
James Muldoon discusses the global supply chains of AI and how people are forming emotional attachments with chatbots.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

James Muldoon is a sociologist who writes about the changing nature of human-technology relationships. Love Machines: How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Our Relationships investigates how people form emotional attachments with large language models, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. Feeding the Machine: The Hidden Human Labor Powering A.I., co-written by fellow researchers Mark Graham and Callum Cant and based on more than a decade of fieldwork, follows Global South workers whose knowledge and labor are the basis of AI tools and assistants.

“A lot of people see artificial intelligence as something that is largely automated, frictionless, and just appears as a useful tool for us. But most of the human hours that go into making artificial intelligence possible are not done in labs in Google or OpenAI. The majority of the work is actually very piecemeal ‘data annotation’ work, which is outsourced to various locations in the Global South, everywhere from India to East Africa to the Philippines,” explains Muldoon.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the production process, consumers are increasingly turning to artificial chatbots to fulfill social needs, incentivizing tech companies to amplify the “addictive and manipulative, controlling behaviors” embedded into their systems to keep users increasingly dependent on their products. “We need much stricter regulation to stop these companies … that can get people hooked and give people harmful and dangerous advice,” says Muldoon.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH: As we continue our discussion on artificial intelligence, we’re going to turn from looking at future risks to some of the present-day impacts on people interacting most closely with the technology: the largely invisible global labor force training AI systems, and the people who’ve turned to AI for companionship that replicates human relationships.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re joined now by the sociologist James Muldoon. He’s a research fellow at the Oxford Internet Institute and affiliated fellow at Yale Law School. His new book is Love Machines: How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Our Relationships. His previous books include Feeding the Machine: The Hidden Human Labor Powering A.I. and Platform Socialism: How to Reclaim Our Digital Future from Big Tech.

I want to start with this issue of the — what you call the “hidden army of workers.” AI just doesn’t come out of a lab. I think most people have no idea what’s happening. Can you explain who this hidden army of workers is around the planet, James?

JAMES MULDOON: Yes, certainly. Thanks for having me on.

A lot of people see artificial intelligence as something that is largely automated, frictionless, and just appears as a useful tool for us. But most of the human hours that go into making artificial intelligence possible are not done in labs in Google or OpenAI. The majority of the work is actually very piecemeal “data annotation” work, which is outsourced to various locations in the Global South, everywhere from India to East Africa to the Philippines, where this data annotation work is undertaken by an army of millions of workers across the globe.

Now, just to give you some context, this data annotation could include something like annotating a street scene for an autonomous vehicle, so drawing a box around what is a tree, what is a child, what is a street sign, so that as you’re training an autonomous vehicle to essentially see the road, the algorithm that powers it will be able to learn the difference between these objects.

And this doesn’t happen on its own or automatically. This requires hundreds and thousands of human labor hours at what I call digital sweatshops, which are located all across the globe, and this is often done in very substandard labor conditions. And the whole process of hiring these workers and outsourcing the work to them really mirrors, in a lot of ways, the outsourcing revolution that happened in manufacturing and IT. And I think when it comes to things like coffee or chocolate or our clothes, I think a lot …

author: Estefa
title: Movilización al Ministerio de Economía: 6 de cada 10 argentinos se endeuda para comer
content:
Foto: Carmel Sabino Yglesias


Hoy a las 14  la CGT, las CTA y la UTEP movilizarán hasta las puertas del Ministerio de Economía para reclamar por el endeudamiento económico de las familias. Pero además, en la concentración confluirán distintas cámaras empresariales de pymes que en el Día del Empresario Nacional saldrán a denunciar el cierre de empresas y reclamar medidas al gobierno nacional. El deterioro continuo del poder adquisitivo y el desajuste estructural entre los salarios y el costo de vida han transformado al endeudamiento familiar en una estrategia forzada de supervivencia en la Argentina. De acuerdo con los datos del Monitor de Opinión Pública (MOP) correspondiente a julio de 2026, elaborado por la consultora Zentrix a nivel nacional, el 61,9% de los encuestados recurrió a tomar algún tipo de deuda durante el último semestre para sostener su economía cotidiana. El fenómeno expone una fractura social severa: dos de cada tres personas agotan la totalidad de sus ingresos antes o exactamente el día 20 del mes, empujando a los hogares a recurrir al crédito, a prestamistas informales y a plataformas fintech que operan con tasas de interés exorbitantes para financiar alimentos de la canasta básica y servicios públicos indispensables. Por Matías Mora Caceres.


Este jueves la CGT, las CTA y la UTEP concentrarán en dos puntos de la ciudad de Buenos Aires, en Paseo Colón y Estados Unidos y en Independencia y Paseo Colón para marchar y confluir frente a las puertas del Ministerio de Economía en Hipólito Yrigoyen 250.

El reclamo es por medidas ante un fenómeno que alarma y crece: el endeudamiento exponencial e inacabable de las familias para comer y pagar necesidades básicas.

 No estarán solos, frente al Ministerio en Plaza de Mayo, distintas cámaras empresariales pymes, en el Día del Empresario Nacional, estarán denunciando y reclamando ante el cierre de empresas y la caída de la actividad. El punto en común, la política económica del gobierno de la Libertad Avanza y sus consencuencias: caída del nivel adquisitivo, deseempleo, informalidad, cierre de empresas, endeudamiento familiar.


Analizamos en este informe los datos arrojados por el

Monitor de Opinión Pública (MOP) correspondiente a julio de 2026, elaborado por la consultora Zentrix.


El punto de partida del endeudamiento masivo reside en la pérdida sistemática de la capacidad de compra frente a la escalada de precios y la desregulación de las tarifas. En el relevamiento de Zentrix,

el 87,4% de los consultados manifiesta que sus ingresos no logran ganarle a la inflación

, una percepción que atraviesa de forma transversal a toda la sociedad. Esta asfixia se traduce en una desconfianza generalizada respecto de las estadísticas públicas: el 67,1% de la población descree de las mediciones de precios oficiales y el 61,8% califica la situación económica general del país como decididamente negativa.


En este marco, la idea de que un empleo formal o regular permite estructurar la vida económica de una familia ha quedado prácticamente desarticulada.

El 86,6% de los encuestados afirma con contundencia que en el escenario actual se necesitan dos o más fuentes de ingreso para llegar a fin de mes.


Esta dinámica de insuficiencia provoca una desorganización mensual, generando una crisis prematuramente. Es así como el 66% de la población se queda sin dinero disponible al llegar al día 20 del mes, mientras que apenas un 9,3% logra alcanzar el cierre del ciclo con alguna capacidad de ahorro. Lo preocupante realmente es la brecha generacional alarmante: los más jóvenes son los que peor la están pasando, entre los jóvenes de 18 a 39 años, el 85,5% ya ha agotado sus recursos antes o durante el día 20, en comparación con el 60,6% registrado en la franja etaria de 40 a 59 años. Los sectores jóvenes no solo perciben menores ingresos en el mercado laboral, sino que carecen por completo de ahorros o activos, lo que los convierte en la población más expuesta a los mecanismos de endeudamiento para cubrir los últimos diez días del mes.


El crédito ha dejado de operar como una palanca de movilidad social ascendente, adquisición de bienes durables o financiamiento de proyectos productivos, en la actualidad, el pasivo se contrae para cubrir gastos corrientes e impostergables:


Insuficiencia de ingresos para gastos elementales:

 El 53,7% de las personas que tomaron deuda en el último semestre declaró haberlo hecho de manera directa porque el sueldo no alcanzó para comprar …

author: A.N.A.
title: Fascismo imaginário, a farsa eleitoral e a crítica anarquista
content:
Uma leitura anarquista das eleições como engrenagem de reprodução do capitalismo e da produção de antagonismos imaginários


Por

 

Rick Afonso-Rocha

 | 

16/04/2026


A crítica anarquista às eleições burguesas, formulada por muitos autores, dentre os quais se destaca Errico Malatesta, incide sobre a própria forma da democracia representativa liberal. Longe de denunciar imperfeições ou desvios, o que se põe à mesa é o reconhecimento e a denúncia de que o processo eleitoral burguês constitui, a um só tempo, mecanismo de reprodução da dominação, de neutralização das contradições, de pacificação da luta de classes e de ocultamento do antagonismo real, inclusive pela maximização de antagonismos imaginários, a saber: 

direita vs. esquerda, família vs. perversão, cristianismo vs. destruição dos valores ocidentais, masculinidade cristã vs. ideologia de gênero, liberdade vs. marxismo cultural 

ou ainda

 retrocesso vs. progressismo, 

fascismo

 vs. liberalismo, direitos humanos vs. barbárie, cidadania vs. servidão

 etc.


Em nossa leitura, a eleição não abre possibilidades. Ao contrário, ela as fecha previamente, organizando a política como escolha controlada entre gestores da mesma ordem. Participar desse circuito não tensiona a exploração. Participar desse circuito legitima a exploração capitalista sob a forma de decisão. Cria-se a ilusão de que fazemos parte do processo, que podemos escolher, que somos nós que decidimos o futuro político e que a política exerce dominância sobre o econômico. E o econômico, mesmo quando pulula em nossas narinas, evidenciando a regra do jogo, é moralizado, reduzido à corrupção de alguns políticos, de modo a mobilizar a esperança no surgimento do eterno novo líder, da nova política, da política como gestão, da política como empreendimento.


O econômico sobredetermina. E não estamos falando de interesses ordinários individuais de alguns representantes das facções burguesas que financiam as eleições. O que vemos é um circo, um teatro. Nada se escolhe. Nada se decide. As eleições são uma farsa. Não exatamente porque são fraudadas. Não existe tal necessidade. A farsa eleitoral diz da ontologia da política burguesa, diz da democracia liberal e dos seus limites estruturais, diz da sua razão de ser e do seu funcionamento no edifício mercantil.


Essa engrenagem depende da produção contínua de uma 

cena de conflito

. A polarização entre projetos institucionalizados funciona como encenação reiterada, na qual tudo aparece em disputa enquanto nada de estrutural se transforma. Nesse sentido, simula-se o antagonismo entre dois polos da institucionalidade burguesa. Sim, entre eles temos divergências em relação ao 

modus operandi

 de gerenciamento da ordem capitalista; temos interesses conflitantes entre as facções burguesas. Mas não há divergência quanto à exploração da classe trabalhadora nem quanto à destruição da natureza. Em tempos de, digamos, 

normalidade institucional

 (sempre temporária, dado as crises estruturais do modo de produção capitalista), esse conflito tende a explorar a linguagem humanista civilizatória, mascarando, necessariamente, sua política estruturante imperialista e colonial. Assume-se uma gramática “politicamente correta”. Fala-se em 

direitos humanos

 e em 

progresso

. As eleições são dominadas por termos técnicos e temas menos “polêmicos”. Pauta-se a segurança pública, o investimento em educação e saúde. E os aspectos morais, via de regra, resumem-se às questões de corrupção e desvio do dinheiro público. No espectro político, emula-se a expansão do centro: centro-direita, centro e centro-esquerda. O discurso neoliberal impõe-se sem a necessidade de simular dissenso. A crítica ao neoliberalismo até é formulada, mas sem a necessidade de simular radicalidade.


Essa encenação, contudo, se intensifica precisamente em tempos de crise. E aqui a 

crise

 ultrapassa a noção de dado econômico; ela comparece como operador discursivo estratégico da exploração capitalista. A 

austeridade

, tal como analisada por Clara Mattei, e a lógica da “

doutrina do choque

“, nos termos de Naomi Klein, não apenas respondem à crise, elas a produzem, a dramatizam, a administram e a exploram como condição de possibilidade para o avanço da ordem capitalista. Por isso, a crise é estruturante ao modo de produção capitalista. Nesse cenário, a ordem do capital fabrica e administra o dissenso. Simula-se uma radicalidade que não ameaça o sistema, mas o estabiliza. Inaugura-se a denúncia de …

author: Harriet Williamson & Simon Childs
title: Revealed: The Chart-Topping Music Producer and Animator Behind a Far-Right AI Rapper
content:
The identities of two men behind an AI-generated far-right rapper who sings about how immigration has broken Britain can be revealed for the first time.


Danny Bones is a sharp-cheekboned skinhead whose music videos show him rapping about the decline of Britain, speeding a deportation van through London and fighting a civil war against the “Islamist Front”.


Since we first wrote about him

, Danny Bones has appeared at an event organised by Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – AKA Tommy Robinson. At his Unite the Kingdom rally in May, Robinson told the crowd that a “war of propaganda” is taking place, before the video for the Danny Bones song ‘This Is England’ was played.


But while Danny Bones’ video was projected onto screens outside parliament, he is entirely fictional.


The AI character and the hyperreal universe he inhabits were created by the Node Project, a shadowy creative agency which shares and monetises Danny Bones content. The identity of the individuals behind the Node Project has never been revealed – until now.


A new investigation by the Bureau for Investigative Journalism (TBIJ) in collaboration with Novara Media has identified a series of links between music producer Denver Bamber and the Node Project. Theo Blackledge, a 3D artist and animator from Liverpool, is another founder of the previously anonymous collective.


Bamber is an established music producer and director of a company. He has built his career off working with predominantly black British grime and rap artists. Expense returns for defunct far-right party Advance UK’s Gorton and Denton byelection candidate, Nick Buckley, show the party paid Bamber’s company to produce videos. A previous version of the Node Project’s online shop privacy policy contained the same address as Bamber’s company.


Bamber confirmed that he and Blackledge founded the Node Project and created Danny Bones.


Blackledge separately confirmed his role with the Node Project, although he is not known to be affiliated with Bamber’s company. Bamber said Blackledge is still involved in the project. “Theo and I founded it and are the co-creative directors, working collaboratively across the project with the wider team,” he said.


Asked about their identities and connection to the project, Bamber said that he and the Blackledge “are the founders of the project and the creators behind Danny Bones. We’ve never hidden behind Danny because we’re worried about backlash or because we think we’re doing anything wrong. It’s because this is an art project and Danny is the face of it.”


Bamber described the pair as “two working-class lads exploring ideas that a lot of British people feel and relate to”.


Building the brand.


Bamber is a music producer, audio engineer and songwriter from Greater Manchester who has worked with some of the biggest names in British hip-hop, grime and drill, including chart-topping Manchester rapper Aitch. He boasts industry credits including Warner Music, UMG, NQ Records, Plug Records and GRM Daily. His songs were streamed 120 million times in 2025.


He predominantly works with black British artists including Manchester rapper Kenzo Str8Drop, Liverpool’s Kasst8 and drill artist Tee Zandos from east London. Some of these artists rap explicitly about racism, police harassment and deprivation.


Blackledge has also worked in the UK rap and grime scene. His 3D animation social media accounts have hundreds of thousands of followers. He has previously edited music videos for grime artists including Aystar and Manga Saint Hilare. His recent content includes stylised animations of real musicians and characters from films and video games. In 2019 Bamber and Blackledge worked together on a music video for rapper Gully Pactzz (now Gul Payne).


Bamber also gives artists the chance to learn from him. A

promotional video

 on Bamber’s TikTok account advertises brand development services for “serious artists only”. For £500, as well as recording music, he helps artists with “branding and identity consultation”.


Danny Bones. Image: The Node Project


Bamber appears to have applied these skills to the creation of Danny Bones, whose slick videos convey clear branding and a consistent identity: an angry young man railing against the decline of the UK, which he blames on immigration.


Since first appearing in late 2025, Danny Bones has built an audience for his far-right political message, with more than half a million Spotify streams and 4.5 million YouTube views.

author: Act for freedom now!
title: Sabotage Against the CEA in Cadarache (France)
content:
Bouches-du-Rhône: Sabotage Against the CEA in Cadarache

On the night of Sunday, May 17, 2026, we sawed through a pylon on the 400,000-volt power line supplying the CEA [French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission] in Cadarache. Unfortunately, there was no short circuit.

A significant chapter in the history of French nuclear power was written in Cadarache. It was there that the nuclear propulsion systems for nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines — the flagship of France’s nuclear deterrent — were developed. Today, the site is home to the ITER project, a nuclear fusion research initiative that hopes to make us swallow the myth of clean, renewable, and infinite energy.

We’ll be told that this action is dangerous, but it is the day-to-day normality of nuclear power that poses the real danger. To avoid any risk of an accident, we have left the other power line supplying the site intact; the site also has its own hydroelectric dam.

The media has kept silent on our action. We would like to take this opportunity to greet all those who are fighting against nuclear power. We are taking advantage of the last days of spring to join the campaign “Hotter Than Nuclear – For a Black Spring in 2026” and greet the other groups that have answered the call. Our thoughts go out to the evicted Gare collective and all those fighting against Cigéo. From basic research to waste disposal — down with the nuclear industry!

In memory of Sara and Sandro, who live on in the struggle!

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Democrats Probe Trump Administration’s Fascist Persecution of Left-Wing Groups
content:
The administration’s repression under NSPM-7 “embody the core characteristics of fascist statecraft,” lawmakers say.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A group of 27 Congressional Democrats is probing the Trump administration over its campaign to suppress and persecute people with left-wing beliefs under National Security Presidential Memorandum-7 (NSPM-7), demanding that officials divulge the breadth of their shadowy suppression campaign.

In a letter led to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Democrats express alarm at the administration’s recent actions to suppress dissenters, which they say “dramatically escalate the Administration’s deliberate and targeted attempts to silence any person, organization, or institution critical of its policies and abuses of power on a global scale.”

The lawmakers point to recent statements from Trump administration officials labelling leftists a “cancer” and “enemies of civilization” during the State Department’s recent anti-left-wing ministerial conference on the “Resurgence of Political Terrorism.” In his speech at the conference, Rubio vowed to dismantle left-wing networks “brick by brick.”

These statements have compounded recent chilling actions from the White House to criminalize left-wing dissent under NSPM-7, which targets anyone the administration deems to express “anti-Americanism,” “anti-capitalism,” or even “anti-Christianity.”

In recent months, the Trump administration has massively escalated the government’s suppression of left-wing individuals and groups. It has pursued maximalist punishments for those accused of, in many cases, simple acts of protest, especially acts in solidarity with both Palestine and immigrants. These punishments have included attempted deportations, disproportionately lengthy prison sentences, intense surveillance, and, in the case of people like Renee Good and Alex Pretti, outright street executions.

“This rhetoric and policy embody the core characteristics of fascist statecraft — using the security apparatus of the state to repress and criminalize political opponents and dissenters rather than specific violent acts,” the lawmakers write. They point out that, in inviting other countries to join their cause, as was the case in the recent ministerial conference, the Trump administration is creating a dangerous global network of governments working together for “transnational repression” of dissent.

The lawmakers demand that the administration officials answer questions about the legal authority behind NSPM-7, specify what left-wing groups they are targeting and how, and provide all documentation related to the implementation of Trump’s memorandum.

The letter was spearheaded by Representatives Delia C. Ramirez (Illinois), Jim McGovern (Massachusetts), and Ayanna Pressley (Massachusetts). Administration officials were given until August 18 to respond to the letter, but missed the deadline, Ramirez’s office says. The lawmakers published the letter in hopes of placing more pressure to elicit a response from the White House.

The letter is one of only a handful of relatively muted actions taken by lawmakers against NSPM-7, despite the massive, far-right threat the memorandum poses to civil liberties in the U.S.

author: Ezra
title: Budapest-Komplex: Die Auslieferung des Antifaschisten Gino an Deutschland verhindern!
content:
Budapest-Komplex: Die Auslieferung des Antifaschisten Gino an Deutschland verhindern!


Gemeinsam mit Dutzenden weiterer Antifaschist*innen wird Gino vorgeworfen, im Februar 2023 in der ungarischen Hauptstadt an körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen mit Nazis beteiligt gewesen zu sein. Die Vorfälle ereigneten sich am Rand der antifaschistischen Gegenproteste gegen den

NS

-verherrlichenden „Tag der Ehre“, das jährlich stattfindende europaweit größte Nazi-Vernetzungstreffen. Das nahm Ungarn zum Anlass, um international zur Treibjagd auf Antifaschist*innen zu blasen – mit tatkräftiger Unterstützung der deutschen Behörden, die insbesondere die aus Deutschland stammenden Beschuldigten und ihr Umfeld mit massiver Kriminalisierung überzogen. Angesichts der staatlichen Verfolgungswut und einer möglichen Auslieferung an Ungarn, wo den Beschuldigten bis zu 24 Jahren Haft drohen, tauchten viele Antifaschist*innen unter.

Erste Höhepunkte der deutschen Verfolgungswelle waren die unrechtmäßige Auslieferung der non-binären Person Maja aus Jena an Ungarn und das erste Unrechtsurteil vor einem deutschen Gericht Ende September 2025, als gegen die Nürnbergerin Hanna fünf Jahren Haft verhängt wurden, obwohl es keine Beweise und kaum Indizien gab. Maja, inzwischen mehr als zwei Jahren unter unmenschlichen Bedingungen im ungarischen Kerker, wurde Anfang des Jahres in Budapest in einem Schauprozess zu acht Jahren Zuchthaus verurteilt – ein Urteil, das noch nicht rechtskräftig ist. In Düsseldorf läuft derzeit das Großverfahren gegen sechs Antifaschist*innen, die im Budapest-Komplex beschuldigt werden. Auch im Dresdner Mammutprozess wird mehreren Angeklagten eine Beteiligung vorgeworfen. Der Großteil der in Deutschland Beschuldigten ist seit Jahren in Untersuchungshaft.

Gino, der in Mailand aufwuchs, aber albanische Staatsangehörigkeit besitzt, lebte zuletzt jahrelang in Finnland. Als ihn die finnischen Behörden auf Betreiben Ungarns kurzzeitig festnahmen und ihm die Auslieferung an Ungarn drohte, floh er nach Frankreich, wo er im November 2024 ebenfalls verhaftet wurde. Die Auslieferungskammer des Pariser Berufungsgerichts lehnte es aber im April 2025 ab, den Antifaschisten an Ungarn zu überstellen, und verwies auf die dortige fehlende Rechtsstaatlichkeit und zu befürchtende Folter. Zugleich stellte die französische Justiz in Frage, ob die hohen Voraussetzungen für eine Auslieferung auf der Grundlage des Europäischen Haftbefehls überhaupt gegeben sind: Dieses Instrument ist nur für besonders schwere Straftaten vorgesehen, nicht aber für Körperverletzungsdelikte.

Nach dieser Schlappe für Ungarn sprangen die deutschen Behörden in die Bresche, erließen Ende 2025 ihrerseits einen Europäischen Haftbefehl gegen Gino und forderten seine Auslieferung. Begründet wird dieser Vorstoß damit, dass zwei der Nazis, die am Rand des Naziaufmarschs in Budapest verletzt worden sein sollen, deutsche Staatsangehörige sind. Faktisch musste das Pariser Gericht denselben Sachverhalt zweimal beurteilen, was großen Unmut hervorrief und dazu führte, dass die Entscheidung mehrfach vertagt wurde.

Mit der heutigen Entscheidung gab das französische Gericht dem Druck aus Deutschland nach: Weder überwies es die Entscheidung an den europäischen Gerichtshof noch forderte es weitere Informationen aus Deutschland an. Stattdessen gab es dem Antrag des Karlsruher Generalbundesanwalts statt und bestimmte, dass Gino in zehn Tagen ausgeliefert werden soll. Dabei kennt das Berufungsgericht das hohe Risiko, dass die deutschen Behörden anschließend Gino an Ungarn ausliefern – sei es direkt nach der Überstellung, sei es nach einem Prozess und mehrjähriger Haft in Deutschland. Die Gefahr ist umso größer, als der Antifaschist weder Deutscher noch

EU

-Bürger ist.

Sein Anwalt kündigte umgehend Rechtsmittel ein, sodass die Entscheidung im September vom Kassationsgericht geprüft werden wird.

„Die heutige Entscheidung des Pariser Berufungsgerichts, Gino nach Deutschland auszuliefern, ist empörend. Damit schließt sich Frankreich der wachsenden Zahl von Staaten an, die Antifaschismus zum Hauptfeind erklärt haben, und leistet der deutsch-ungarischen Verfolgungsoffensive Vorschub“, erklärte Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Wir stehen an der Seite von Gino und allen anderen verfolgten Antifas. Seine Auslieferung an Deutschland muss mit allen Kräften verhindert werden. Wir rufen dazu auf, gegen dieses Urteil zu protestieren: Wir sind alle Antifa – no extradition!“ …

author: Unknown
title: Martyr Culture
content:
This essay was generously written by Sara Blum, an internationalist who spent several years with the YPJ in Rojava, published 2025.


„I remain committed, until the end, to the struggle for liberation


and to the beauty and love it creates.“


Abdullah Öcalan


Kurdish friends, upon meeting an internationalist, often ask about our decision to come to their homeland in Rojava, Kurdistan. When they'd ask how I first came into contact with the friends, I felt a bit embarrassed to say that, honestly, the first friends of the movement I met were those who helped me after I actually arrived in Mesopotamia. (Editor's note: “The friends” is a colloquialism stemming from the literal translation of the word “heval” which has historically been used by members of the Kurdish liberation movement to refer to each other.) I told them I learned about the movement by reading articles on a few different anarchist websites and contacted the friends by email. In fact, I knew so little about the movement that I first emailed YPG (People's Protection Units) instead of YPJ (Women's Protection Units). The friends were often amazed at this, and in their generosity considered it some kind of bravery or indication of the depth of my belief in the revolution and the people, rather than of naivety or impulsivity. It's a common story among internationalists from the so-called USA, because the Kurdish Freedom Movement doesn't have a presence here like it does in many parts of Europe, where there is a bigger Kurdish diaspora. When I initially went, I planned to stay for six months or a year. I ended up staying for several years, and for most of that time I was with the autonomous women's military defense forces, YPJ.


I decided to go in late 2018, and at that time it was hard to find much information about what to expect. Not much has changed in that regard. My dad told me to bring extra socks, and that before going I must read Che Guevara's On Guerrilla Warfare. Other than that, most of the practical information about what to bring I received from an internationalist fighter whom I reached through an online message board. He said to bring all sorts of supplies, sent a packing list, and told me to bring a bunch of US dollars. He emphasized that I should bring water for border crossing across the mountains, which he said would be long and difficult, but to not share my water because the Kurdish comrades would pass it down the line until there was none left, and then I wouldn't have water. The YPJ friend I was corresponding with told me I didn't need much, and if it came to be that I needed something when I got there or along the way, comrades would sort it out then. This seemed to me rather casual at the time. I felt frustrated at the vagueness.


Packing and repacking my bag, researching the weather conditions, trying to prepare as much as possible for what could be the rest of my short little life, I wanted all the information I could find and there wasn't much. I didn't realize then that I was encountering the first contrast of revolutionary and capitalist culture: different modes of being. The internationalist from the message board, with his best intentions, showed me one way to go about struggle, while the YPJ comrade showed me another way of joining the revolution. Preparing myself as an individual by making sure I had all the right specific things on the one hand, and on the other, preparing myself to take on the same circumstances as whomever I end up with and to sort all my needs within the context of our collective needs. As an internationalist from the West, the tension between these tendencies has long lived in me. I find that it still does, but I have also found that being out of water together always seems to be better than having water while the person next to me doesn't.


Before I left, I tried many times to write letters to my family, close friends, and comrades, which I would leave in the hands of a trusted friend so that, in the event of my death, they could be sent. I was determined to leave loved ones with some words of strength—I didn't want to die, but since it was a distinct possibility, it was important to ensure that my death would not be a weight or darkness in their lives. I had made this decision for myself, but I realized as time went on that I'd also made a decision for many other people. My mother became the mother of a YPJ fighter defending the Women's Revolution. My close friends in the U.S. became personally …
