title: Solon, groups decry systemic failures in Zamboanga school shooting
content:
Children should not be compromised by budget cuts. Schools should have enough guidance counselors, nurses, and support personnel.

LAGUNA – Children and teachers’ advocacy groups criticized institutional failure in the wake of the August 18 shooting incident at the Ateneo de Zamboanga University (AdZU), Zamboanga City that left two dead, including the shooter.

An initial report from the Philippine National Police (PNP) identified the alleged shooter as a Grade 9 student of the Ateneo de Zamboanga University (AdZU). The victim was a Grade 10 student of the same school. Both fatalities were minors.

ACT Teachers Partylist Rep. Antonio Tinio raised questions as to how the shooter gained access to a gun, where it came from, and who is responsible for keeping the weapon.

Tinio also demanded for a House investigation with regard to school violence after the Zamboanga City shooting. “Children should not be compromised by budget cuts. Schools should have enough guidance counselors, nurses, and support personnel,” he said in Filipino.

Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns stated that this shooting is an “undeniable manifestation of the rapidly collapsing state of children’s welfare in the country.” The children’s alliance also criticized the current administration’s lack of preemptive measures against school shootings.

“The children are not at fault, it is the rotten system who is at fault. Instead of proposing comprehensive and pro-people solutions for children’s rights, the government chooses to point fingers at the victims while neglecting their duties,” said Salinlahi Secretary General Elle Buntag in Filipino.

For her part, Alliance of Concerned Teachers Philippines (ACT) Chairperson Ruby Bernardo decried Presidential Communications’ Office Undersecretary Claire Castro calling teachers as “the ones teaching ill manners to students.”

“Our elected officials, including those in the Malacañang, should be the models [of right conduct] but the public only see them committing corrupt practices, stealing funds and evading accountability,” Bernardo said in Filipino. She stressed that the government should be examples for the youth.

Buntag also criticized Castro’s statement. “Teachers keep our education system alive despite hunger and their measly salaries, then you go around and evade responsibility over your own institutional failure? Do not make teachers the punching bags of your negligence.”

Kabataan Partylist said that since June 2026, there have been five reported cases of school violence in the country. “These are manifestations of the lack of support and protection provided to the youth in terms of mental health services, economic support, and accessible and quality education.”

In a statement, the Commission on Human Rights said that these incidents require a nuanced view on juvenile justice and child protection. “A rights-based juvenile system holds children accountable in ways appropriate to their age and development, while recognizing that children involved in violence may themselves require protection and intervention.” (AMU, DAA)

title: Women want workshops for men responsible for violence
content:
The Diyarbakır (Amed) Metropolitan Municipality Women’s Department and district municipalities are meeting with women in rural neighborhoods to raise awareness of violence against women and femicide. As part of the initiative, workshops have been held in 22 villages, focusing on the different dimensions of violence and possible solutions.


The initiative, organized as part of the “Our word is not over, we will stop violence together” campaign, has been underway for nearly two years. The work has revealed that women face not only physical violence but also various forms of economic, psychological and digital violence.


At workshops held in villages and district centers, women discuss the forms of violence they experience and put forward their demands for solutions. Sociologist Eylem Kaya, who is involved in the fieldwork, spoke to ANF about her observations.


 


Kaya said they document the violence and other problems women face and work to develop solutions. She noted that women in rural areas tend to define violence primarily in terms of physical abuse, while other forms of violence often go unrecognized. Kaya said women face various forms of violence, adding: “Women want us to focus on solutions rather than simply talking about the problems.”


Women are unaware of the violence they experience


Eylem Kaya said that during their meetings, some women initially told them, “There is no violence here. We never come across such stories.” However, once different forms of violence were discussed, women began to reassess their own experiences.


Kaya said the workshops addressed economic and psychological violence as well as the burden of unpaid care work in the home: “Once we discuss how the burden of domestic care falls entirely on women, how this creates profound inequality and can also lead to psychological violence, women begin to define their experiences differently.”


Some women have no access to healthcare


Kaya said women also face violations in access to healthcare, education and infrastructure: “Even when women in the villages we visited did not raise these issues themselves, we made a point of bringing them up. It made us see once again how heavy the responsibilities and burdens they carry are. This allowed us to make the inequality even more visible.


As I said, women genuinely cannot access healthcare. In one village we visited, for example, there was a case of hepatitis, but they were unaware of it. There is no functioning health center. There is a health center, but no doctor working there. They cannot travel back and forth to the city center because transportation is extremely difficult.


When the requests we receive fall within the municipality’s responsibilities, we try to address them. If they concern another department, we document them, refer them to the relevant unit and follow up at regular intervals.”


Digital violence manifests itself in every sphere


Eylem Kaya said their training sessions on digital violence against women and safe internet use had challenged assumptions that older women were unlikely to experience digital violence. She noted that sessions on digital violence had become some of the longest parts of the workshops.


Kaya said: “We initially received a request for training on digital violence and safe internet use for women, so we went and held the training. Both we and some of our colleagues there had certain preconceptions. We thought that because the women attending were older, they probably did not use social media or platforms such as WhatsApp, Instagram or TikTok. But when we got there, the session on digital violence ended up being our longest.”


Kaya stressed that digital violence affects people of all ages, particularly women and girls: “The experiences they shared with us showed us once again that this is a form of violence and that people of all ages can be subjected to digital violence, particularly girls and women. Recently, we have been focusing specifically on one form of violence. It was an issue we initially approached with some preconceptions, but one that later surprised us greatly: digital violence.”


Kaya said different forms of violence could not be considered in isolation, as the conditions in which women live directly affect both the form and extent of the violence they experience.


Kaya also said: “Violence is so multidimensional and takes so many forms that it varies according to the particular circumstances of each village. In some villages …

„… In Argentinien kämpft nur eine sehr überschaubare Anzahl von Umweltschützern vor Ort und die Mapuche-Indianer dagegen. „Obwohl wir laut Gesetz ein Recht auf Anhörung haben, werden wir nicht einmal informiert, wenn eine Erdölfirma unser Land besetzt“, so Jorge Nahuel, Koordinator der Mapuche Konföderation. „Heute sind Erdbeben Alltag“, sagt Hernán Scandizzo von der Beobachtungsstelle Erdölfragen im Süden, „die Regierung von Neuquén wie die (nationale Erdölfirma) YPF machen die Kritik am Fracking lächerlich. Sie verweigern jede Diskussion. Wenn sie doch darüber sprechen, dann nur über das, was auf der Erd-Oberfläche passiert, wenn die Häuser einstürzen. Aber sie verschweigen die Konsequenzen dieser Beben auf das unterirdische Rohr-System.“  (…) Als es immer häufiger bebte, begann Professor Javier Grosso, die Daten mit den Aktivitäten der Erdölfirmen zu vergleichen

.“…“ – aus dem

Bericht „Argentinien: Fracking am Ende?“ von Gaby Weber am 25. Februar 2020 bei telepolis


 über das angebliche neue El Dorado Argentiniens und die langen Auseinandersetzungen um dieses „Projekt“…


Tote Wale für deutsches Gas in Argentinien: Flüssigerdgas-Terminals in Patagonien finanziert durch deutsche Kreditgeber bedrohen ein ganzes Ökosystem


„Im Golfo San Matías sind regelmäßig zahlreiche Meeressäuger zu beobachten. Der Bau von Gasterminals und Ankerpunkten für sechs riesige Transportschiffe könnte zerstörerische Auswirkungen auf ein wichtiges Ökosystem und enormen Einfluss auf den Klimawandel haben. (…)


Seit etwa vier Jahren importiert Deutschland Flüssigerdgas über schwimmende LNG-Terminals. LNG steht für „Liquefied Natural Gas“ (Flüssigerdgas) und gelangt derzeit hauptsächlich aus den USA, wo es durch Fracking gewonnen wird, über Norddeutschland in deutsche Haushalte. Mit Beginn des Krieges zwischen Russland und der Ukraine hatte die Bundesrepublik begonnen, Alternativen für russische Gaslieferungen zu suchen. Nun zeichnet sich eine ähnliche Tendenz durch Spannungen zwischen den USA und Europa ab. In diesem Kontext hat der deutsche staatliche Energieversorger Sefe mit dem argentinischen Konzern Southern Energy eine Liefervereinbarung über acht Jahre getroffen, um ab 2027 LNG zu importieren. Die deutsche Bundesregierung muss jetzt entscheiden, ob sie für den dafür notwendigen Ausbau der Infrastruktur im Golfo San Matías in Patagonien eine ungebundene Finanzkredit-Garantie (UFG) erteilen will, wie die deutsche NGO urgewald berichtet. Urgewald geht davon aus, dass hinter der Voranfrage zur UFG die Deutsche Bank steckt: Sie sei bereits maßgeblich an einem Kredit in Höhe von zwei Milliarden US-Dollar für eine Öl- und eine Gaspipeline beteiligt, die vom gigantischen Vaca-Muerta-Fracking-Gebiet an die Küste des Golfo San Matías verlaufen soll – in der gleichen Region, in der auch die LNG-Lieferinfrastruktur für das genannte LNG-Geschäft für Sefe entstehe, heißt es in einer Pressemitteilung der NGO. In Argentinien regt sich derweil Protest. Im März 2025 gründete sich die Kampagne „Golfo Azul Para Siempre“ (etwa: „Blauer Golf für immer“). Als Teil der Organisation Fundación Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (Stiftung für Umwelt und natürliche Ressourcen, Farn) setzt sie sich gegen den Ausbau der Infrastruktur am Hafen von Punta Colorada sowie gegen den Bau zweier Pipelines – einer für Öl und einer für Gas – von Vaca Muerta zum Atlantik ein. Ein Schwerpunkt ihrer Arbeit ist es, Einfluss auf potenzielle Kreditgeber der Projekte zu nehmen. (…)


Nicht nur würde sich Argentinien über Jahrzehnte von fossilen Strukturen und Exporten abhängig machen. Das Hauptproblem für die Kampagne liegt in der maßlosen Umweltzerstörung, die mit den schwimmenden Gasterminals, dem aufkommenden Schiffsverkehr und potenziellem Austreten von Öl und Gas einherginge. Das Gas müsste für den Transport verflüssigt werden. Das würde in großen, schwimmenden Tanks geschehen, in die kaltes Meerwasser eingespeist und nach dem Prozess mit höherer Temperatur wieder ins Meer geleitet würde. Sechs Terminals sind dafür in Planung. Das ist nicht nur kritisch, was die Klimaerwärmung angeht. Es ist ein problematisches Unterfangen für ein Ökosystem mit großer Artenvielfalt: Im Golf leben schützenswerte Tiere, wie Glattwale, Magellan-Pinguine, Delfine und Seepferdchen, die zur Fortpflanzung regelmäßig in den Golf kommen. title: Tanhan: Öcalan's status must be clarified for lasting solution
content:
Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) MP Kamuran Tanhan spoke to ANF about the scope and legal nature of the Framework Law, saying that although the legislation has shortcomings, it will serve as a “framework and foundational law” on which subsequent legal arrangements will be based. Tanhan said the boards to be established under Article 7 would play a decisive role in implementing the process and that comprehensive amendments would therefore be needed to the Anti-Terror Law, as well as legislation governing the execution of sentences and criminal procedure.


Tanhan said the legislation should be regarded, in legal terms, as a starting point and a reference text: “The Framework Law has shortcomings. A framework law will naturally leave many issues unresolved. Since this is a framework and foundational law, all subsequent legislation will refer back to it. In that respect, it is, of course, important. The fact that it is a standalone law is significant in itself.”


Tanhan said it was not possible to regulate every provision within a single law, adding that the legislation sets out the basic parameters within which subsequent arrangements will take shape: “Of course, this legislation has many shortcomings, but there is also a principle in legal reasoning: it is not always possible to include everything in a single law. Sometimes a framework or boundaries are established, and further arrangements are made within those boundaries. There are certainly shortcomings. For example, it refers to the decisions and case law of the Constitutional Court and the European Court of Human Rights. There is no fundamental return to a legal framework based on the rule of law. The fact that the law deals only with the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and the process of ending the armed struggle is, of course, also a shortcoming.”


Board under Article 7 will take a position according to the course of the process


Tanhan assessed the implementation of the Framework Law, drawing particular attention to the board envisaged under Article 7. He said the board, which will include senior representatives from the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Justice, and the security and intelligence bureaucracy, would play a decisive role in implementing the process and shaping future legislation.


Tanhan said the board would have broad powers and that its decisions would also provide a basis for new legislation to be brought before Parliament: “Senior officials from the state's security and bureaucratic institutions, including the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Justice and the National Intelligence Organization, will form a board and meet periodically to make assessments. This board will have broad powers. Its recommendations will likely shape judicial and administrative arrangements, particularly legislation to be enacted by Parliament. In other words, the process will take shape on the basis of those decisions.


Depending on how the process develops, that board, or rather the boards under Article 7, will take a position accordingly. If the process continues as they want or develops positively, it will of course produce positive results. But if the process does not proceed in the way they want, this could also lead to measures directed entirely against Kurdish politics.”


The Anti-Terror Law must be abolished entirely


Tanhan stressed that the reforms required after the Framework Law should cover a broader legal field, particularly the Anti-Terror Law and legislation governing the execution of sentences. He said the Kurdish question had for many years been addressed through security policies and criminal law: “For this reason, the Anti-Terror Law must be abolished in its entirety, along with changes to the law on the execution of sentences. As the DEM Party, and indeed as the Kurdish people, we have maintained from the outset that the demands of the Kurdish people and demands concerning the Kurdish question, including demands for democracy, have always been suppressed under the guise of combating terrorism, while rights have been violated. It was through this legal framework, through the Anti-Terror Law, that the Kurdish Freedom Movement and the Kurdish struggle were equated with terrorism. We have always argued that this law must be abolished entirely, and we continue to do so today.


However, it appears that they will not abolish the law altogether. According to their reasoning, there are also structures …

title: Ερωτευτήκαμε τη φωτιά (Ντοκιμαντέρ για την εξέγερση στη Χιλή το 2019)
content:
το αρχείο του υποτίτλου στα ελληνικά εδώ

Δυο λόγια με αφορμή τον υποτιτλισμό στο ντοκιμαντέρ “Fell in Love with Fire – A Documentary about the 2019 Uprising in Chile”

https://crimethinc.com/2024/10/21/fell-in-love-with-fire-an-documentary-about-the-2019-uprising-in-chile

Η ανάγκη να δώσουμε λόγο στα δεινά είναι η προϋπόθεση της αλήθειας. Διότι τα δεινά είναι η αντικειμενικότητα που βαρύνει το υποκείμενο. Αυτό που βιώνει ως απολύτως υποκειμενικό, είναι αντικειμενικά διαμεσολαβημένο.

~Τεοντόρ Αντόρνο, «Αρνητική διαλεκτική»

Η Χιλή αποτελεί μια χώρα-κλειδί για την κατανόηση της πολιτικής βαρύτητας του δυτικού ιμπεριαλισμού: Οι στρατιωτικές επιχειρήσεις και τα γεωπολιτικά συμφέροντα απαιτούν παράλληλα και εξαγωγή δημοκρατίας· Δημοκρατία ως πολιτική έκφραση του κεφαλαίου, που στο όνομα της εκλογικής συμμετοχής θα εφαρμόζει τις πιο βάρβαρες πολιτικές.

Η Χιλή, όπως και η Ελλάδα, αποτελούν παραδείγματα κρατών όπου ο εκδημοκρατισμός χρειάστηκε μια αμερικανόφερτη χούντα – εκεί ο Πινοσέτ, εδώ οι συνταγματάρχες.

Το εργαστήρι του νεοφιλελευθερισμού υπήρξε η Χιλή, όπου η σχολή του Σικάγο έκανε τις πρώτες δοκιμές πάνω στη λατινοαμερικάνικη ιδιαιτερότητα.

Από τη δικτατορία Πινοσέτ στην «επιστροφή στη δημοκρατία» της δεκαετίας του ‘90, και από εκεί στους κοινωνικούς αγώνες των πρώτων δεκαετιών του 2000 με τη νεολαία στην πρώτη γραμμή. Η εξέγερση του Οκτώβρη του 2019 αποτέλεσε έναν φάρο για τους αγωνιζόμενους σε όλο τον κόσμο, σε μια περίοδο εντεινόμενης διεθνούς πόλωσης, λίγο πριν η πανδημία του covid «ανακόψει» το κύμα ταραχών που είχε απλωθεί στις διάφορες γειτονιές του πλανήτη, από το Hong Kong, το Ιράν και τον Λίβανο, ως τη Γαλλία και τη Χιλή.

Σήμερα, στον απόηχο της εξέγερσης, είναι εμφανής η αδυναμία του χιλιανού επαναστατικού κινήματος να αποτρέψει την αφομοίωση των εξεγερμένων στον σοσιαλδημοκρατικό κρατισμό. Μετά τις πρόσφατες εκλογές στα τέλη του 2025, το κράτος της Χιλής, υπό την ακροδεξιά διακυβέρνηση Καστ, ετοιμάζεται να πατήσει πάνω στη συντριβή των κοινωνικών αντιστάσεων, βαδίζοντας στον δρόμο που έστρωσε η «προοδευτική» ελπίδα – ακόμα μια ομοιότητα με την εδώ πραγματικότητα.

Ακολουθούν κάποιες αναλυτικές επισημάνσεις για την FMPR και τον Camillo Catrillanca, γιατί κρίναμε πως η ιστορία τους αξίζει λίγη παραπάνω έκταση – παραπάνω από μια απλή αναφορά των ονομάτων μέσα στο ντοκιμαντέρ.

Η FMPR (Frente Patriotico Manuel Rodriguez) γνωστή κι ως Frente (Μέτωπο), ήταν μαρξιστική/εθνικoαπελευθερωτική ένοπλη οργάνωση στη Χιλή πρωτοεμφανιζόμενη τον Δεκέμβρη του 1983, όταν ανατινάχτηκαν δώδεκα πύργοι μετάδοσης υψηλής τάσης, αφήνοντας το κεντρικό τμήμα της χώρας στο σκοτάδι. Το 1987, το μεγαλύτερο μέρος της, αποσχίζεται από το κομμουνιστικό κόμμα Χιλής, συνεχίζοντας ως FMPR-Autónomo τον ένοπλο αγώνα και μετά το τέλος της δικτατορίας του Πινοσέτ. Στο απόγειο της πολύμορφης δράσης της αριθμούσε πάνω από 4.000 μέλη, έχοντας χιλιάδες ενέργειες με εκρηκτικές επιθέσεις, σαμποτάζ στον κρατικό μηχανισμό και σε καπιταλιστικούς στόχους, απαγωγές και εκτελέσεις αστυνομικών, στρατιωτικών και πολιτικών, ληστείες τραπεζών, απαλλοτριώσεις και ένοπλες περιφρουρήσεις κινητοποιήσεων. Το 1996 υλοποιείται απόδραση τεσσάρων κρατούμενων της οργάνωσης με ελικόπτερο, από φυλακή υψίστης ασφαλείας του Σαντιάγκο, με την συνδρομή ανταρτισσών του ΙΡΑ (Ιρλανδικός Δημοκρατικός Στρατός).

Ο 24χρονος Camillo Catrillanca, δολοφονήθηκε στις 14/11/2018 από την GOPE ή αλλιώς κομάντος της ζούγκλας, με σφαίρα στο πίσω μέρος του λαιμού έπειτα από επιχείρηση της αστυνομίας στη περιοχή Temucuicui, καθώς οδηγούσε ένα τρακτέρ. Η δολοφονία του έρχεται στα πλαίσια κλιμάκωσης του μακροχρόνιου πολέμου που διεξάγει η κρατική εξουσία στις αυτόχθονες κοινότητες, και της ευρύτερης καταστολής και στρατιωτικοποίησης του νότιου τμήματος της Χιλής. Το Temucuicui είναι περιοχή που απαρτίζεται από κοινότητες των Μapuche, ένα εμβληματικό μέρος αντίστασης απέναντι στα συμφέροντα του κράτους, των εταιρειών και των μεγαλοκτηματιών.

title: Damascus government's demands stall integration process
content:
Relations between Rojava and Damascus have seen intense activity in recent days. Talks between the Autonomous Administration and the Damascus government are continuing, while tensions on the ground are also rising. Attacks on the first convoy to return to Serêkaniyê after seven years and the killing of two fighters in Qamishlo have raised questions over whether the integration process has reached an impasse.


An agreement signed on 29 January between the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and the Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) administration in Damascus included key provisions on implementing a ceasefire, integrating the structures of the Autonomous Administration into the central system while preserving them, ensuring the safe return of people forcibly displaced from occupied areas, recognizing the language and identity rights of Kurds, and restructuring the security system.


More than six months later, however, education in the mother tongue, the return of forcibly displaced people and the status of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) remain among the main obstacles to progress on the agreement. Rather than accepting and recognizing the Kurds’ fundamental demands, the Damascus government continues to impose a centralized, uniform approach.


These issues were also discussed at a meeting in Damascus on 4 August between SDF Commander-in-Chief Mazloum Abdi, Autonomous Administration Department of Foreign Relations Co-Chair Ilham Ahmed and interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa (Al-Jolani).


Softening' on Kurdish-language education


Kurdish-language education and the status of the Kurdish language were among the most important issues discussed at the meeting. The Damascus government once again insisted that Kurdish be taught only as a two-hour elective course, a proposal rejected by the Rojava delegation. Talks on the issue are expected to continue with the Ministry of Education, while Damascus is said to have “softened” its position somewhat compared with previous discussions.


Damascus seeks to deploy forces in Kobanê


One of the key sticking points in the agreement is who will be responsible for security in Kobanê. Security in Kobanê is currently provided by Kurdish forces, while Damascus forces are stationed in Şêxler, Çelebiyê and Sirrin. The Damascus government is seeking to deploy its forces in Kobanê, but the SDF have rejected the proposal.


Dispute over limiting the number of fighters


The status of SDF fighters deemed “surplus” is another contentious issue in the integration process. More specifically, the Damascus government wants to consolidate the fighters into four brigades and limit their overall number, a move aimed at weakening the Kurdish defense forces.


The SDF currently has three brigades in the Cizirê Region and one in Kobanê. Damascus wants to limit each brigade to 1,300 fighters and disband those it considers “surplus.” However, disagreements over the number of fighters mean that the SDF integration process cannot yet be considered complete. The SDF continues to insist that all of its fighters be included in the process.


YPJ to remain as an 'anti-terrorism force'


The status of the YPJ remains one of the most closely watched issues in the integration process. Since taking power in December 2024, HTS has refused to recognize the women fighters as an autonomous force and has sought their dissolution. The YPJ, however, has maintained that it will continue to fulfil its responsibility to defend the people as a women’s force.


According to information provided by Hassan Mohamed Ali, Co-Chair of the General Relations Office of the Syrian Democratic Council (SDC), the issue was also discussed at the latest meeting in Damascus. A proposal was put forward for the YPJ to remain in place not as a force within the Syrian army, but as an “anti-terrorism force” affiliated with the Ministry of Interior. A final decision is expected to be made in talks between the YPJ and the Ministry of Interior.


List of names requested for international representation


Kurds are also seeking a role in Syria’s international representation. The Rojava delegation reportedly said at the latest meeting that Kurdish representation should extend to consulates and embassies. At present, Kurds hold few senior positions beyond the post of Deputy Defence Minister, Deputy Commander of the 60th Division, the Hasakah (Hesekê) Governorate and several directorates. The delegation stressed that Kurds are one of the peoples who should have …

author: Vivian La
title: US Army Corps approves a pipeline project it knows harms Indigenous lands
content:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers issued a key permit for a plan to update an aging segment of the Line 5 pipeline crossing the Straits of Mackinac in Michigan, the waterways that tribal nations say are central to their ways of life.


It’s a procedural win for Line 5 owner Enbridge Energy, but comes amid ongoing legal and regulatory hurdles at the state level that prevent the start of construction. The pipeline carries oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles from Superior, Wisconsin, through Michigan to Sarnia, Ontario, and Enbridge wants to replace a 4-mile segment that lays on the bottom of the ecologically sensitive straits with a new one, buried in a tunnel under the lakebed.


In a statement issued with the decision, the Army Corps said the project wasn’t contrary to the public interest, complied with Clean Water Act guidelines, and “would not abrogate or impermissibly impair tribal treaty rights.” Review of the permit was fast-tracked under President Donald Trump’s executive order last year declaring a “

national energy emergency

.”


For Michigan tribes that have fought for years to shut down the pipeline, the federal permit approval was “disrespectful and ludicrous,” said Austin Lowes, chairman of the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians.


“They’re acutely aware of the impact that this project will have on Indian Country, and they just flat-out ignored it,” Lowes said. “It’s one of the most disgusting things that I’ve ever been confronted with as a tribal leader.”


According

to the Army Corps itself

, tunnel construction would have permanent adverse impacts on wetlands, vegetation, land use, and cultural resources. The straits are

sacred

 to Anishaabe peoples — the waters feature prominently in their creation story and serve as burial grounds for ancestors. Five tribal nations also hold treaty rights to fish and hunt in these waters, rights that predate Michigan’s statehood and are protected by federal law under the 1836 Treaty of Washington.


“Us surrendering and ceding that land came with certain expectations and rights,” Lowes said. “And one of those expectations was that we would be consulted any time decisions were going to be made on the federal level that would impact our way of life, and the tunnel project certainly does that.”


The agency determined that despite any negative impacts on surrounding lands and property, the proposed tunnel would reduce the environmental risks associated with the pipeline, such as leaks caused by a direct hit from a boat’s anchor. “The benefits of the project outweigh its detriments,” the Army Corps stated. Its scope of analysis was focused on the construction impacts, and not the risk of an oil spill or greenhouse gas emissions beyond the tunnel site, which the

agency said

 is the responsibility of the federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration.


Last year, seven Michigan tribal nations

withdrew from discussion

 with the Army Corps over the permit, saying that regulators ignored tribal expertise, input, and concerns, and undermined treaty rights. The withdrawal also came after the Army Corps suggested that the review process would likely be fast-tracked under President Trump’s emergency executive order.


“A project that’s going to take somewhere between six and 10 years to build is certainly not a response to a national energy emergency, and it won’t change the amount of fossil fuels transported,” said Debbie Chizewar, managing attorney at Earthjustice, a legal nonprofit supporting Michigan tribes in litigation against Enbridge.


The Army Corps’ “flawed” review likely has wider impacts for all tribal nations, said David Gover, who is Pawnee and Choctaw and a managing attorney at the Native American Rights Fund, which is supporting Earthjustice.


“This notion that, ‘Yeah, we understand that this will permanently destroy your resting relatives, but we don’t care, and we got to move ahead. We got to have these fossil fuels’ — that challenges tribal sovereignty,” Gover said.


Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy said in a statement that the permit approval is “a significant step forward” for the project, and reflects years of “rigorous review” from the federal agency. The company “is committed to protecting the Great Lakes, the region’s natural and cultural resources, and the waterfront communities that depend on them, while also ensuring reliable energy for the region,” the statement said.


Even with a federal stamp of approval …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: ‘2027 national budget deprioritizes the poor’
content:
Some physical copies of the proposed 2027 P7.2-trillion National Expenditure Program (NEP) submitted by the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) to Congress on August 11, 2026. Photo from DBM

How will Marcos fund the P7.2 trillion national budget when 2027 revenue collection is projected to be only at P5.206 trillion?

CAGAYAN DE ORO — The state’s budget department described the proposed P7.2-trillion 2027 national budget as “people-centered.” But for progressive legislators, it deprioritizes the Filipino people.

On August 11, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) submitted the proposed 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP) to Congress. Lawmakers belonging to the Makabayan bloc criticized the state’s massive allocations on infrastructure projects despite the flood control scam while reducing the allocation in social services.

DBM allocated P739.02 billion—the largest allocation under economic services—to fund various infrastructure programs of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the Department of Transportation (DOTr) for 2027. This is 46.37 percent higher than the 2026 budget allocation.

Meanwhile, a total of P187.95 billion was allocated next year for water resources development and flood control, which is 19.01 percent higher than this year’s budget. A huge portion of the amount (P103.45 billion) will fund the Flood Management Program of DPWH, the government agency criticized over the anomalous flood control mess.

“History and recent experience have repeatedly shown that infrastructure funds are the lifeblood of bureaucratic corruption and political patronage,” party-list representatives Antonio Tinio of ACT Teachers, Sarah Jane Elago of Gabriela, and Renee Co of Kabataan said in a joint statement.

Read: ‘Selective prosecution’ in Marcos Jr. anti-corruption probe?

Tinio demanded the total removal of allocations in flood control projects. This should be used, he said, to build more classrooms instead. “How can the Marcos Jr. administration fulfill its promise of 40,000 classrooms before his term ends if the target for next year is only 700?”

The Department of Education’s (DepEd) proposed budget shows that only 700 new classrooms were targeted for 2027, which is much lower compared to its target of 4,869 new classrooms this year. The classroom shortage reportedly stood at more than 160,000 units.

The proposed 2027 NEP is 5.99 percent higher compared to this year’s national budget of P6.7 trillion. Social services remain the highest allocation (P2.456 trillion), but this is lower by P143.72 billion compared to this year.

Under social services, the housing and community development sector suffered the largest cut. From its P7.86 billion allocation this year, it was reduced to P6.82 billion next year, or a 37% decrease. This was followed by the health sector, which suffered a 20.87% decrease.

All sectors under social services have decreased their allocations, except the subsidy to local government units (LGUs).

Renato Reyes Jr., president of the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), criticized the allocation of P1.143 trillion, or 15.87 percent of the proposed 2027 national budget, for debt payments, as this was higher compared to DepEd’s allocation.

“How will Marcos fund the P7.2 trillion national budget when 2027 revenue collection is projected to be only at P5.206 trillion?” Reyes asked in a Facebook post.

DepEd remains the highest allocation (P976.0 billion) among all departments but this is still lower compared to its P1.015 trillion budget this year. It was followed by DPWH and the Department of Health (DOH), which includes PhilHealth and specialty hospitals.

Both Reyes and the Makabayan bloc criticized the more than P4.5 billion confidential and intelligence funds (CIFs) of the Office of the President.

“Why are we against the existence of confidential and intelligence funds? Because no matter how ‘stringent’ the existing guidelines, the proponents of the CIF are able to circumvent the guidelines and abuse the funds,” Reyes said. “Any funding that is lump-sum and discretionary is simply pork barrel and gives rise to corruption.”

The House of Representatives has just started to discuss the 2027 national budget. The Makabayan bloc lawmakers vowed to oppose what they called an “anti-people budget.” (DAA)

Sînorê hejariyê 122 hezar e


Li ser bingeha sînorê birçîbûnê û bi hîmgirtina lêçûnên serfkirinê yên malbatan, sînorê hejariyê jî wekî 122 hezar û 217 lîre hatiye diyarkirin.


Lêçûna mehane ya xurekên ku ji bo xwarineke tendurist û hevseng a mêrekî mezin pêwîst dike, 10 hezar û 25 lîre hatiye diyarkirin.


Ev yek ji bo jineke mezin 9 hezar û 649 lîre, ji bo ciwanekî 15-18 salî 10 hezar û 473 lîre û ji bo zarokekî 4-6 salî jî 7 hezar û 57 lîre ye.


Di nav lêçûnên rojane yên tebaxê de, bi 431,31 lîreyan barê herî giran ket ser milê şîr û berhemên şîr. Li pey vê, bi lêçûna 288,82 lîreyan koma sebze û fêkî tê.


Goştê sor, masî û mirîşk bi 209,80 lîreyan bû komeke din a girîng a xurekê ku di lêçûnan de derdikeve pêş.


Lêçûna ku ji bo hêkan pêwîst dike jî wekî 24,90 lîreyan hatiye diyarkirin.


Ev pere ji bo dexl û danê hişk 28,87 lîre; ji bo koma birinc, savar, meqarne û arvan 19,14 lîre; ji bo nan 86,67 lîre; ji bo rûn û zeytê 78,43 lîre û ji bo şekir, hingiv, rîçal û dimsê jî 43,98 lîre ye.


(AY)

title: Arslan: Turkey must share central powers with local governments - Part Two
content:
In this ANF interview, Mehmet Arslan, former Co-Chair of the Democratic Regions Party (DBP), talked about the struggle for local democracy in Turkey and Switzerland's models of cantonal governance and referendums. Arslan offered assessments on a wide range of issues, from the European Charter of Local Self-Government and trustee policies to the role of young people in politics and social peace.


The first part of this interview can be read

here

. 


You have been in Switzerland for around three years and have observed local government practices in different cantons. How do Switzerland's federal structure and cantonal system contribute to strengthening local governments? What impression has the model of direct participation here made on you?


When you first arrive in Switzerland, you are surprised in a sense. As someone who has been involved in politics for many years, you think you have an understanding of developments around the world, but Switzerland has a very distinctive structure. There are 26 cantons here, with 26 different models of decentralized governance. Although there is a federal parliament, legislation can vary from canton to canton and even from municipality to municipality.


In Turkey, municipal legislation is the same in Diyarbakır as it is in Istanbul or Ankara; everything is governed through a uniform approach. In Switzerland, however, even a municipality in the smallest settlement can make decisions according to its own specific circumstances.


For example, when I spoke to people living in a village in the canton of Zurich, they told me that their electricity bills were higher than elsewhere. When I asked why, they said, “This is an affluent area. The community itself chose to share this cost so that the municipality could provide better services.” In other words, decisions are shaped through mechanisms in which people discuss issues directly and convey their decisions to the councils.


Here, the state is not an instrument of pressure over society but a mechanism for resolving problems through collective cooperation with the people. This semi-militia system, in which people participate directly in politics and shape decision-making processes, provides an extremely important model of how local democracy should function.


You mentioned Switzerland's commune and cantonal structures. We know that even people without official positions take responsibility in local processes within this system. How is public participation in decision-making mechanisms reflected at the institutional level?


Citizens who hold no official position or title can become directly involved in local government issues. They can contribute to resolving problems by putting forward ideas and developing projects.


Here, proposals developed through semi-militia structures, communes or the people's own efforts to find solutions are presented to the relevant official bodies once they have matured, where they are turned into projects and given legal status. From the outside, the system may appear to operate informally, but across Switzerland's 26 cantons, people participate directly in governance, providing a genuine example of people-oriented municipal governance.


Since each of the 26 cantons operates independently, it is impossible to say, “I know Swiss legislation in its entirety.” Each canton has its own forms of participation. This diversity does not create confusion; on the contrary, it enriches democracy and strengthens the will of the people rather than the central structure.


For example, a recent debate in the federal parliament on limiting the country's population to 10 million was taken to a referendum by the people and was not approved. This is a concrete indication of how actively society can participate in politics. Switzerland's model of local government offers a distinctive experience in which social problems are resolved directly through cooperation between assemblies and the people, without being constrained by centralization.


When models of decentralized governance are discussed in Turkey, it is often argued that they would “create confusion”, “undermine the country's unity” or “lead to disorder”. Does the Swiss model, extending from the Gemeinde/commune level to the cantons and the federal confederation, create confusion? How does this system preserve the will of different national groups to live together?


The most valuable aspect of Swiss democracy is that decisions are not made solely through the …

title: ÇHD says that prisoners were tortured in Antalya S-Type prison
content:
The Antalya Branch of the Contemporary Lawyers’ Association (ÇHD) said that prisoners at Antalya S-Type Prison had been subjected to beatings and torture by prison guards. The statement recalled that operations had been carried out across Turkey in connection with the NATO Summit held in July, and that more than 50 people had been detained in Antalya. The statement said that three of those detained had been remanded in custody, adding: “Following reports from prisoners in other wards, the prisoners in question were visited and signs of torture on their bodies were observed.”


Dragged along the ground for 200 metres


The statement continued with the following account of what happened: “On the morning of 13 August 2026, prisoners held at Antalya S-Type Prison were subjected to an arbitrary attempt to impose a standing roll call, which they opposed. It was reported that a large number of guards then entered the ward and courtyard, and that the prisoners were subjected to severe beatings. The prisoners were subsequently taken out of the ward and dragged along the ground for approximately 200 metres before being taken to an area referred to by prison administrators as a ‘temporary ward’. The prisoners were subjected to torture there as well.”


Marks of torture documented


ÇHD said that the marks of torture on the prisoners’ bodies were still visible and that the injuries had been documented and recorded in official reports. The statement said that, at the prisoners’ request, they were taken to a health facility, where they were examined and described what they had experienced, including the torture to which they had been subjected. However, it said the prisoners were not allowed to see the medical reports issued following their examinations.


 ÇHD to file criminal complaint


ÇHD said it would file criminal complaints against all forms of rights violations committed against the prisoners, adding: “We hereby inform the public that we will continue to follow up this process until those responsible for this crime are punished.”

author: Dalia Gebrial
title: We Lost Jason Arday to a Moral Panic
content:
Professor Jason Arday’s life was precious and important. It ended prematurely following a callous, industrial-scale media witch hunt. For all the talk of the facts, many facts about his life have come to light since his passing. That he was widely regarded as a gentle man, a mentor to a number of young scholars and someone whose research was deeply impactful. Facts that turn him from a villain into a multi-dimensional human being. Even if he hadn’t been those things, he wouldn’t have deserved what happened to him – but they’re worth noting at the outset. May he rest in peace and power. 


We’re living in an era of far-right populism. Far-right populism rests on the belief that only a specific kind of life is valuable and legitimate. In order to strengthen support for that belief, its champions have to consistently make the case that other lives aren’t valuable or legitimate. 


One of the key mechanisms through which the right makes that case is via media-fuelled moral panics: by finding a story through which its particular targeted community can be located as the origin of all of society’s ills. Sometimes that story has a grain of truth to it; often it’s entirely falsified. But the right takes that story and blasts it so aggressively into people’s consciousness that it becomes almost impossible to see the world in any other way. 


These moral panics – whether they’re about ‘diversity, equity and inclusion’ (DEI), ‘woke’ taking all the good jobs from the people who deserve them, trans people using bathrooms or competing in sports, or refugees seeking shelter – dehumanise these communities to the point where it then seems entirely logical to enact violence and expulsion upon them. After all, if a group of people is causing social decay or ill, they should be removed, right? 


The role of a critical media outlet in this context is to have enough media literacy to understand when that machine is in motion, and to identify

that

 as the story worth covering.

That

 is the story of how power is operating.

That

is the story in the public interest. Point blank period. 


Because when it comes to the facts of this case, there were many that weren’t part of the discussion, deliberately. Here are just a few. 


First, as

Ash Sarkar has pointed out

, many people in academia, media and government have faced credible allegations of not just plagiarism, but far, far more serious kinds of academic misconduct. People who are public figures, who hold state power. Those allegations got at best a day of coverage. Many didn’t result in job losses, and none in a media frenzy so extreme as that we’ve seen over the last few weeks. Nor did those allegations turn into a wider discussion about the right of people with the same identity to hold positions of influence. That’s because those people are white and powerful. 


Second, the university is in crisis, but it’s not because of DEI. There was no pearl clutching about the integrity of the academy when it was being compromised by the

closure of entire departments overnight

,

mass redundancies

 and

substantial funding cuts

 – because there’s no moral panic there. Instead, the undermining of the social contract of the university – like the social contract of Britain today – was placed at the feet of one man and all he represents. What does he represent? The ‘DEI hire’ – an accusation that no person of colour is safe from. 


Third, we’re living in an age of far-right populism, which rests on the scapegoating and dehumanisation of people of colour and all people marked by their identity as unworthy and undeserving of dignity. That context is also a fact. 


Within that context, decisions to dig up and pass comment on every facet of Arday’s personal and professional history – from old lectures to former students – added to the pretension that, several days into what was clearly a disproportionate, racially charged onslaught, the story was still about Arday himself. Those of us interested in challenging power should have been clearer about what was unfolding before our eyes. 


I’m concerned about how some of my fellow Novara Media contributors have responded to the frenzied hounding of Arday over the last fortnight, which I believe reflects a general rightward drift in British culture that has been followed by parts of the left. I’ve been concerned for a while. We need to work harder to immunise ourselves against this drift, and to be much more wary of a press that isn’t …

author: Brian Hioe
title: Lai Administration Takes A Page Out of KMT’s Playbook with Cash Handouts
content:
THE LAI ADMINISTRATION has announced plans for cash handouts of 10,000 NT to the general public. The Lai administration has framed this as sharing the dividends of Taiwan’s AI boom with the general public, stating that Taiwan had reached the highest economic growth in 39 years.

If this spending amount is approved in the 2027 budget, then the distributions will take place next year. In this sense, one observes several aims by the Lai administration with calls for the cash handout. For one, cash handouts have proven popular with the public in the past, such as those often advanced by the KMT. But the Lai administration is also hoping to add to public pressure to pass the 2027 budget, which the KMT has delayed on for months.

For its part, the KMT seems to know that Lai is taking a page out of its playbook. The KMT has thus criticized Lai for a “double standard” in that the KMT previously proposed a 10,000 NT cash handout in May, but this was then criticized by the Executive Yuan, which stressed fiscal discipline. Now, the KMT has called for the doubling of the cash handout to 20,000 NT.

This is similar to last year, when the legislature also pushed for cash handouts of 10,000 NT. Though the Lai administration resisted the idea, it later reversed course to try and take credit for it.

In particular, with the KMT continuing to seek drastic cuts to funding for sections of government, as it also did in past years, it may be that the public does not understand when social services are cut. Instead, the public may simply prefer cash handouts. Indeed, it is expected that cultural funding will continue to take a hit in the budget, even as the KMT has downplayed the cuts and suggested that its actions are, in fact, generous to the Lai administration. In the meantime, the KMT has also continued to hit out at the funding allocated to DPP politicians, including Lai and Premier Cho Jung-tai. Recent actions by the KMT in the legislature include cutting 10 million NT from Lai’s annual discretionary budget and freezing the remaining 20 million NT, as well as freezing Cho’s salary from September through December 2026.

The Executive Yuan and Legislative Yuan have also continued to be at loggerheads over child saving legislation, with Cho refusing to countersign. This is the sixth time that Cho has refused to countersign legislation since December 2025, a move that appropriated a veto power to the Executive Yuan that did not previously exist, and was likely to push the KMT on the issue of their freeze of the Constitutional Court. The bill would require the government to deposit 60,000 NT per year into a savings account for eligible children under 8, and 30,000 NT for children between 7 and 17, who would also receive 30,000 NT in another account annually.

But the legislation allows for “corporate sponsorship” funds, which has been accused by the Lai administration of being murky, seeing as this could allow wealthy families to accrue more money. The Lai administration declining to countersign the bill, citing the constitutional principle of proportionality, was on this basis. Budgeting contention between the DPP and KMT continues, then.
